subheadings.label: Background and succession
facts: Henry had issued his Third Act of Succession in 1543. This confirmed that if Edward died without heirs the throne would pass to Mary and then Elizabeth.
The religious and factional struggles of the latter years of Henry's reign had left a divided council between the reformists and the conservatives.

subheadings.label: The problem of Edward's minority
facts: When Edward became King in January 1547 there were serious concerns about his age. He was only nine when he came to the throne. It was feared that a regent might be appointed, that Edward wouldn't be able to control faction within the Council, and that the image of monarchy as a strong, divine power would be challenged by the image of a child.

subheadings.label: Historical precedent
facts: Previous minorities had ended badly. In 1483 Richard III had seized power during his nephew's minority, and the young princes disappeared in the Tower.

subheadings.label: Henry's solution: the Regency Council
facts: Henry, fearing the negative influence of a single regent, instructed in his will that a Regency Council of 16 members should be formed, balanced between the reformists such as Seymour and conservatives led by Gardiner and Norfolk.

subheadings.label: Why the solution failed
facts: However in the last year of Henry's life Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant the Council was no longer balanced, but weighted in favour of the reformists.

Following Henry's death Seymour and Paget conspired using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will to increase their power. Seymour was made Duke of Somerset, Lord Protector and predominant figure on the new Regency Council.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Edward's age have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: Edward was only nine and could not control faction within the Council.
DID: The image of monarchy as strong and divine was challenged by a child king.
DID: Historical precedent of Richard III's minority showed how dangerous minorities could be.
DID: Henry's carefully balanced Council immediately collapsed - weighted toward reformists.
DID: Seymour and Paget exploited Henry's will to seize power, creating exactly the situation Henry feared.
DIDN'T: Henry anticipated the danger and tried to prevent it with a balanced 16-member Council.
DIDN'T: The Regency Council system did function to provide government during the minority.

subheadings.label: Henry's intentions
facts: Faction in government is not inevitably a destabilising force for monarchs. Other Tudor monarchs encouraged faction to ensure their ministers competed for their loyalty.
However, faction in the reign of a minor was more dangerous as there was no authority to control it. Factional disputes could spill over into rebellion or civil war.

subheadings.label: Factions on the Council
facts: Factions on the Council were initially defined in terms of religion: reformists and conservatives. Key reformers included Somerset and John Dudley, Earl of Warwick. Key conservatives included Thomas Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton.

subheadings.label: Somerset's domination
facts: The reformist faction, led by Somerset, dominated the Regency Council by 1547. He gave positions to supporters like his brother Thomas Seymour, who he later executed for treason.
As Lord Protector he was able to use the position to increase his personal wealth and power, which resulted in criticism from opponents and even former supporters.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the Regency Council have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: Faction in a minor's reign was more dangerous as there was no authority to control it - could spill over into rebellion or civil war.
DID: The reformist faction dominated the Council by 1547, undermining Henry's intended balance.
DID: Somerset gave positions to supporters and executed his own brother Thomas Seymour for treason.
DID: Somerset used his position to increase personal wealth and power, attracting criticism.
DIDN'T: Faction is not inevitably destabilising - other Tudor monarchs encouraged it for competing loyalty.
DIDN'T: The Council continued to govern despite factional disputes - it didn't collapse into rebellion or civil war.

subheadings.label: Why faction turned against him
facts: Somerset's arrogant and dominating leadership created a new faction: the Anti-Somerset faction. This was a combination of reformers and conservatives including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget, the man who had helped Somerset's rise to power.
They also feared Somerset's apparent sympathy for the commoners and the problem of enclosure. They believed this sympathy had encouraged the unrest of the summer of 1549.
Edward himself disliked Somerset's control as he was allowed no influence at all.

subheadings.label: Events of his fall
facts: The unrest of 1549 weakened Somerset's hold of power as many in the Council blamed his policies. Several, including Paget, wrote to Somerset criticising his leadership.

Feeling threatened, Somerset took possession of Edward and on the 5th October issued a general summons for all loyal subjects to defend the King and himself against the Council. This was seen as inciting revolt.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: On the 6th Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle but was forced to surrender to the Council when the King turned against him, declaring he was being kept a prisoner by Somerset. Somerset was arrested.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Somerset's fall have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: His fall revealed deep factional tensions within the Council - reformers and conservatives uniting against him.
DID: The unrest of 1549 had already weakened government before his fall, showing instability.
DID: Somerset's attempt to rally subjects against the Council on 5th October was an act of incitement that could have led to civil war.
DID: The fall demonstrated how vulnerable government was when a minor was on the throne.
DIDN'T: The transfer of power happened relatively peacefully - Somerset surrendered rather than fighting.
DIDN'T: Edward himself supported the change, giving it legitimacy.
DIDN'T: The Council quickly reorganised under Northumberland - government continued without major disruption.

subheadings.label: How he secured power
facts: Following Somerset's fall there was a power vacuum on the Regency Council. Warwick's role in the defeat of both the Western and Kett's rebellions had made him politically indispensable — he was seen as a strong leader who could restore order.

Facing opposition from conservatives including the Earls of Arundel and Southampton, Warwick allied himself with the reformist faction and committed to further religious reform — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550 and Duke of Northumberland.

He released Somerset and restored him to the Council in the hope he would use his influence to stabilise the regime — but when this failed, Somerset was arrested again and executed for treason in January 1552.
The evidence suggests the accusations of treason against Somerset were fabricated — Northumberland needed to remove the one figure who could plausibly challenge his dominance of the Council.

subheadings.label: Assessment of his rule
facts: Northumberland's methods showed how dangerous minority rule was — without a strong monarch, the most ruthless faction could dominate government and eliminate opponents under cover of law. Edward himself was becoming more active in government by 1552–53, aged 14–15.

Northumberland promoted rapid Protestant reform under Stage 3 — the Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) and Forty-Two Articles — partly out of genuine conviction but also to cement his alliance with the reformist faction.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Northumberland's rise have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: He executed Somerset on fabricated treason charges, removing his only credible challenger - a sign of unstable factional politics.
DID: His rise demonstrated how the most ruthless faction could dominate government during a minority.
DID: His commitment to rapid Protestant reform was partly factional positioning, not just conviction - religion became weaponised in factional politics.
DID: His unilateral elimination of opponents 'under cover of law' undermined rule of law.
DIDN'T: He restored order after the rebellions of 1549 - Warwick's victories at the Western Rebellion and Kett's made him 'politically indispensable'.
DIDN'T: He attempted reconciliation by releasing Somerset and restoring him to the Council.
DIDN'T: Edward was becoming more active in government by 1552-53 - the regime was moving toward more stable monarchical rule.

subheadings.label: Why it was devised
facts: In early 1553 Edward VI's health began to decline causing anxiety about the succession. Edward himself was concerned for the survival of the radical Protestant changes he so valued.
Henry VIII had stipulated in the Third Act of Succession that if Edward died without children the throne would pass to Mary Tudor.
Mary was a committed Catholic and had maintained her faith throughout Edward's reign. Even Edward's personal appeals could not move her. Mary's accession would lead to the restoration of Catholicism.
Northumberland was concerned for his own power. He knew that his role in government would lead to his fall from power when Mary came to the throne.
There is debate about who was more responsible in developing the Devise — Edward was 15 and taking a far more active role in government by 1553.

subheadings.label: What it proposed
facts: The Devise for the Succession was written naming the future male children of Jane Grey as Edward's heirs. To preserve his power, Northumberland married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey, hoping to control the heir.
However Edward's illness progressed rapidly before Jane Grey had children. In his own hand Edward crossed out the phrase 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey herself as his heir.
Edward died on 6th July 1553. His death was kept quiet for 2 days whilst prominent nobles were pressured to sign the Devise.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: Mary acted quickly. She had a significant power base in East Anglia and quickly dispatched riders to proclaim herself Queen. The Council proclaimed Jane on the 10th, after Mary's proclamation on the 9th.

Mary raised a large force of supporters. Northumberland left London to face Mary but on the way many of his army deserted him and the Councillors who had been forced to support the Devise broke ranks. Northumberland retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary was queen on the 19th.

Mary triumphantly entered London to rousing support. She released Gardiner and Norfolk from jail and showed leniency towards many who opposed her. However, Northumberland, Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all later executed.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the Devise have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: It was an unprecedented attempt to overturn Henry VIII's legitimate succession by manipulating a dying child king.
DID: Edward's death was concealed for 2 days while nobles were pressured to sign - a constitutional crisis.
DID: Northumberland's marriage of Guildford to Jane Grey was a transparent power grab.
DID: It triggered a succession crisis that needed military mobilization to resolve.
DIDN'T: Mary's victory was swift and decisive - the Devise collapsed within days.
DIDN'T: There was no civil war - Northumberland's army deserted rather than fight.
DIDN'T: Mary showed leniency in victory, demonstrating political wisdom that stabilised the realm.
DIDN'T: Most people accepted hereditary succession - the Devise had no legal basis and was rejected.

subheadings.label: The Devise and its motives
facts: The Lady Jane Grey affair grew directly out of the Devise for the Succession. Edward VI and Northumberland feared that Mary's accession would mean the restoration of Catholicism and the end of Northumberland's power. The Devise named Jane Grey — a Protestant great-niece of Henry VIII — as Edward's heir, bypassing both Mary and Elizabeth.

Northumberland strengthened his grip by marrying Jane to his son Guildford Dudley in May 1553. When Edward died on 6th July 1553, his death was kept secret for two days whilst prominent nobles were pressured to sign the Devise. The Council then proclaimed Jane as Queen on 10th July.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: Mary acted immediately and decisively. She had a significant power base in East Anglia and quickly dispatched riders to proclaim herself Queen, calling for support from loyal subjects and her cousin Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor. Many of the gentry and nobility rallied to Mary — not necessarily out of Catholic sympathy but out of respect for legitimate hereditary succession.

Northumberland left London to face Mary with an army but many of his troops deserted him. Councillors who had been forced to sign the Devise broke ranks and declared for Mary. Northumberland retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary was Queen on 19th July 1553. The affair had lasted just nine days.

The Devise had no legal basis and went against Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession. Most people believed in hereditary succession as divinely ordained. Mary's gender was seen as less important than the principle of legitimate succession. Northumberland had overreached — he lacked the popular support that Somerset had at least initially enjoyed.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Northumberland, Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all executed. Mary released Gardiner and Norfolk from jail and showed leniency towards many who had opposed her — demonstrating political judgement. The failure of the Devise showed that attempts to manipulate the succession without popular or noble backing were doomed.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the Jane Grey affair have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: It was an unprecedented challenge to legitimate succession after Henry VIII's Third Act.
DID: It required military mobilization and threatened civil war.
DID: It resulted in multiple executions - Northumberland, Jane Grey, Guildford Dudley.
DID: It exposed how a determined faction could attempt to seize the throne.
DIDN'T: The whole affair lasted only nine days - resolved very quickly.
DIDN'T: There was no civil war - troops deserted to Mary rather than fight.
DIDN'T: Mary's leniency towards opponents demonstrated political wisdom that stabilised the realm.
DIDN'T: The principle of hereditary succession was reinforced, not weakened.

subheadings.label: Why it was seen as a problem
facts: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right.
In the 12th century, Matilda, daughter of Henry I, was named as heir to the throne. Following Henry's death there was a civil war as many nobles refused to accept Matilda.
Henry VIII's determination to gain a male heir shows the anxieties of leaving the realm to a female ruler.
Many believed female rulers would not be able to control powerful men in their government, lead soldiers into battle or display the power and strength that a monarch needed to epitomise.

Radical Protestants viewed female rulers as unnatural. John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, comparing female rulers to the 'blind leading those who can see'.

subheadings.label: Why it mattered less than feared
facts: However, the willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen suggests issues of gender were seen as less important compared to religion.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Mary's gender have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right - unprecedented.
DID: Historical precedent of Matilda's contested succession showed female rule could trigger civil war.
DID: Henry VIII's obsession with a male heir shows the deep anxieties around female rule.
DID: Many believed women couldn't control men, lead armies, or display monarchical power.
DID: Radical Protestants like John Knox attacked the very concept of female rule.
DIDN'T: Edward and Northumberland were willing to make Jane Grey queen - showing religion mattered more than gender.
DIDN'T: Mary successfully secured the throne despite her gender, defeating the Devise.

subheadings.label: Why it was controversial
facts: Mary needed to marry to create an heir to ensure the longevity of her Catholic restoration. However, issues were raised about the suitor.

If Mary married an English noble this would lead to division and faction within court and Council. If Mary married a foreign prince this could lead to an unpopular influx of foreigners and England's entanglement in foreign wars.

Two major candidates emerged: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon, championed by Stephen Gardiner; and Philip of Spain, championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice. Philip would bring powerful diplomatic alliances as his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain. However, it risked a xenophobic popular reaction.

subheadings.label: How it was managed
facts: Fearing a negative reaction, a treaty was agreed by the Spanish representatives and Parliament to avoid instability. It was agreed that: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England; after Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars.
Despite reassurances, Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January 1554, ostensibly in reaction to the marriage to Philip.
Ultimately, the marriage ended unhappily. After Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent any time in England. When Mary died Philip commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Mary's marriage have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: It triggered Wyatt's rebellion in January 1554 - actual armed rebellion against the regime.
DID: It risked xenophobic popular reaction against foreign influence.
DID: It risked entangling England in Spain's wars - exactly what the treaty tried to prevent.
DID: Mary's phantom pregnancy raised hopes of a Catholic heir that were dashed - leaving succession unclear.
DID: Philip's lack of presence in England left Mary without consort support.
DIDN'T: A treaty was successfully negotiated to limit Philip's power - he was named King but had no real authority.
DIDN'T: The treaty's restrictions (no Spaniards in office, no claim after Mary's death, no involvement in Spain's wars) were largely respected.
DIDN'T: Wyatt's rebellion was defeated and didn't overthrow Mary.

subheadings.label: Mary's management of Council
facts: One of the key criticisms of female rulers was that they would not be able to control the male ministers in their government, leading to damaging factional struggles. Mary was keen to ensure an efficient and streamlined administration: casual councillors were excluded from key committees in 1554; in 1555 Mary established an inner council so only her most valued advisors were present.
Mary's Council was dominated by three key figures: Stephen Gardiner (Bishop of Winchester) - a committed Catholic reformer.
Reginald Pole was sent as Papal Legate, working with Gardiner to push aggressive Catholic restoration.
William Paget represented the moderate faction, urging caution in religious change to avoid destabilizing the realm.

subheadings.label: The Paget-Gardiner rivalry
facts: The Paget-Gardiner rivalry was the central factional conflict of Mary's reign. They divided over two issues: Mary's marriage and the pace of the Catholic restoration. Gardiner championed the English suitor Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon; Paget championed Philip of Spain, knowing he was Mary's preferred choice and hoping to gain favour. Paget won this argument.

On religion, Gardiner and Pole were diametrically opposed. Gardiner stressed caution and persuasion — he opposed the heresy burnings as counter-productive and believed moderate Catholics should be accommodated. Pole favoured dramatic change backed by persecution. Gardiner's death in November 1555 ended his moderating influence; the burnings increased rapidly under Pole's direction from 1555 onwards.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: Despite Council divisions, Mary's councillors worked effectively together for most of her reign.
They successfully carried out her wishes, including the Marian persecutions and Spanish marriage.
The Council's effectiveness showed that factional disputes did not prevent coordinated policy implementation.

The factional conflict between Paget and Gardiner ultimately mattered less than the structural problem of Mary's reign — the failure to produce an heir. Factional disputes about the pace of religious change were resolved by death (Gardiner) and departure (Philip). The real crisis was dynastic, not factional.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Marian faction have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: The Paget-Gardiner rivalry was 'the central factional conflict of Mary's reign'.
DID: Council divisions over Mary's marriage and pace of Catholic restoration shaped major policy.
DID: Gardiner's death in 1555 ended his moderating influence - burnings increased rapidly under Pole.
DID: Factional divisions affected the pace and severity of the Catholic restoration.
DIDN'T: Mary streamlined administration - excluded casual councillors and established inner council in 1555.
DIDN'T: Despite divisions, councillors 'worked effectively together for most of her reign'.
DIDN'T: They 'successfully carried out her wishes' including persecutions and Spanish marriage.
DIDN'T: The real crisis was dynastic (failure to produce heir), not factional.

subheadings.label: Problems Elizabeth inherited
facts: Mary died on 17th November 1558. Cardinal Pole died on the same day, leaving the Church of England without an Archbishop of Canterbury.
Mary had failed to produce an heir. Her phantom pregnancy in 1555 had raised hopes that were quickly dashed, and Philip had largely abandoned England after 1555.
England had also suffered the humiliation of losing Calais in 1558, the last English territory in France, as a consequence of Mary's decision to join Spain's war against France.

subheadings.label: The international situation
facts: The succession passed peacefully to Elizabeth. Philip of Spain, despite having the power to press a claim, chose not to. He recognised Elizabeth as Queen, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.
Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate, due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce.
The papal view that Elizabeth was illegitimate made her succession problematic for Catholic powers.
This religious illegitimacy strengthened the position of Mary, Queen of Scots as a potential alternative heir.
Elizabeth therefore inherited not just a country divided by religion, weakened by war and debt, but an immediate Catholic challenge to the legitimacy of her rule.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the 1558 succession have serious impact on stability?
facts: DID: Mary's death left England without an Archbishop of Canterbury (Pole died same day).
DID: Mary had failed to produce a Catholic heir, leaving Catholicism vulnerable.
DID: Loss of Calais in 1558 was a national humiliation.
DID: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate.
DID: Mary Queen of Scots had a strong alternative claim.
DID: Elizabeth inherited religious division, war and debt.
DIDN'T: The succession passed peacefully to Elizabeth - no civil war.
DIDN'T: Philip of Spain recognised Elizabeth as Queen and chose not to press a claim.
DIDN'T: Philip preferred Protestant England to French-aligned Catholic one - international situation stabilised.

subheadings.label: Henry VIII's legacy
facts: Despite Henry VIII's Break from Rome in 1534, Henry never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced Protestant changes that would bring him money and power, most notably the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–41).

The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic doctrine including Transubstantiation, clerical celibacy, private masses and auricular confession — England was doctrinally Catholic despite the break with Rome.

The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, likely did not fully understand the differences between Catholicism and Protestantism and just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium.

subheadings.label: The Council in 1547
facts: Henry left a divided council — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant it was already weighted in favour of the reformists before Edward came to the throne, making further Protestant reform likely.

subheadings.label: Doctrinal confusion
facts: The repeal of the Act of Six Articles under Somerset in 1547 opened the door to radical Protestant preaching. Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all being preached, creating confusion about what the official doctrine actually was.

subheadings.label: The legacy of the Dissolution
facts: The Dissolution of the Monasteries had removed a key source of Catholic charitable provision and community — but it had also created a powerful vested interest among the gentry who had bought monastic land and would resist any Catholic restoration that threatened their property.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Henry's religious legacy radical or limited?
facts: RADICAL: Henry broke from Rome in 1534 - a fundamental constitutional and religious change.
RADICAL: Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536-41) removed a major Catholic institution.
RADICAL: Council was already weighted toward reformists by 1546 (Gardiner and Norfolk had fallen) - further Protestant reform likely.
RADICAL: Dissolution created vested interests among gentry who bought monastic land - would resist Catholic restoration.
RADICAL: Repeal of Six Articles in 1547 opened door to Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism.
LIMITED: Henry 'never truly embraced Protestantism' - only changes that brought money and power.
LIMITED: 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic doctrine - England remained doctrinally Catholic.
LIMITED: Most of country outside London and East Anglia didn't understand the differences.
LIMITED: People 'just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium'.

subheadings.label: The overall approach
facts: The leading architects of radical change, Archbishop Cranmer and Somerset, had to act slowly. Before they could install their new religion, the old had to be destroyed.

subheadings.label: Stage 1 - Destruction: Legislation
facts: Repeal of the Six Articles removed the Catholic doctrine set out by Henry.
Repeal of the Treason Act meant it was no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.

subheadings.label: Stage 1 - Destruction: Iconoclasm
facts: Royal injunctions were issued encouraging iconoclasm in churches across England.

subheadings.label: Stage 1 - Destruction: The Chantries
facts: Dissolution of the Chantries that were seen as superstitious forms of Catholic worship. Also brought in a lot of revenue and land for the Crown.

subheadings.label: Stage 2 - Limbo 1548–49
facts: Stage 2 – Limbo, 1548–49: The repeal of the Treason Laws opened up a Pandora's Box of new radical ideas. Various versions of radical Protestantism were being preached including Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism.

In December 1548, Cranmer published his First Book of Common Prayer. This was enforced nationwide in the First Act of Uniformity. It was a compromise between the old and the new and did not please anyone. Notably it was extremely vague on the stance on Holy Communion. This Prayer Book prompted rebellion in the West Country.

subheadings.label: Stage 3 - Formulation 1550–53
facts: Stage 3 – Formulation, 1550–53: Following Northumberland's rise the pace of religious reform increased. A new ordinal was introduced in 1550, allowing leading Catholic clergy to be deprived of their positions and replaced with Protestants.

In 1552, Cranmer published the Second Book of Common Prayer, enforced by the second Act of Uniformity. This was much more radical and unambiguous than the first. It removed all Catholic practices, and confirmed Calvin's doctrine that Communion was purely symbolic.
In 1552, the Forty-Two Articles, outlining the key doctrines of Edward's Church, were drawn up. Edward's death in 1553 ensured these Articles were never passed by Parliament.
Nevertheless, by 1553, de jure England was a Protestant country.

subheadings.label: Debate: What was the extent of religious change under Edward?
facts: EXTENSIVE: Complete destruction of Catholic religion - images destroyed, Chantries dissolved.
EXTENSIVE: Six Articles (Henry's Catholic doctrine) entirely repealed.
EXTENSIVE: Treason laws repealed to allow open preaching of Protestant doctrine.
EXTENSIVE: Royal injunctions systematically enforced iconoclasm nationwide.
EXTENSIVE: The Second Prayer Book removed ALL Catholic practices.
EXTENSIVE: Calvin's doctrine of purely symbolic Communion confirmed.
EXTENSIVE: Forty-Two Articles drafted to outline completely new Protestant doctrines.
EXTENSIVE: By 1553, England was de jure a Protestant country.
LIMITED: Stage 1 destruction had to be 'slow' - showing caution and resistance.
LIMITED: The First Prayer Book was deliberately a compromise that 'did not please anyone'.
LIMITED: It was so vague on Holy Communion that it sparked rebellion in the West Country.
LIMITED: Northumberland's rise was needed to accelerate reform - earlier phase was hesitant.
LIMITED: Edward's death meant the Forty-Two Articles were never passed by Parliament.
LIMITED: Financial motives mixed with religious (Chantries dissolution brought revenue).

subheadings.label: Limited time for change
facts: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true nationally. Edward's rule lasted six years — in an age when ideas spread slowly this was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship. The early caution showed by the government (e.g. Cranmer's First Book of Common Prayer) shows they anticipated opposition.

There was little time for the more radical policies to have an impact. The Second Act of Uniformity and 42 Articles were only in the last months of Edward's reign. The repeated efforts to remove icons and conduct visitations prove the lack of uniformity — the changes were hard to enforce at parish level.

subheadings.label: Local compliance was superficial
facts: At a local level compliance was patchy and often superficial. Many parishes simply removed images and altars when required but continued private Catholic devotion. Evidence from people's wills shows little support for the Protestant changes except in London, the south-east and East Anglia. Many people simply conformed outwardly because they were told to — without any genuine conversion.

subheadings.label: Clerical resistance and ignorance
facts: Clerical resistance and ignorance was a major obstacle. In his visitations around his diocese of Gloucester, Bishop Hooper reported that of 311 clergymen, 171 were unable to repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer. The government had been unable to train enough Protestant clergy to replace those who resisted change.

subheadings.label: Local opposition and rebellion
facts: Popular opposition broke out most dramatically in the Western Rebellion of 1549, led by clergy objecting to the First Prayer Book.
The Prayer Book was in English rather than Latin, which alarmed traditionalists who saw it as Protestant innovation.
The Western Rebellion showed that even 'gentle reform' faced serious resistance from the common people.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: The rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary might suggest that traditional religion still retained its popularity, particularly in the North and West. However it is equally possible that this simply reflects local willingness to conform to whatever the government required — the same passive obedience that had enabled the Edwardian reforms in the first place.

subheadings.label: Debate: What was the extent of de facto change under Edward?
facts: LIMITED: Edward's rule lasted only six years - small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
LIMITED: Local compliance was 'patchy and often superficial' - parishes continued private Catholic devotion.
LIMITED: Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes except London, south-east, East Anglia.
LIMITED: Bishop Hooper found 171 of 311 clergymen unable to repeat Ten Commandments, 40 couldn't find Lord's Prayer.
LIMITED: Popular opposition broke out in Western Rebellion of 1549 against First Prayer Book.
LIMITED: Government couldn't train enough Protestant clergy to replace those who resisted.
LIMITED: Rapid Catholic restoration under Mary suggests traditional religion retained popularity.
EXTENSIVE: De jure England was Protestant by 1553 - all major legislation in place.
EXTENSIVE: People conformed outwardly even without genuine conversion - same obedience that enabled reform.
EXTENSIVE: Despite resistance, government did push through major changes including Two Prayer Books.

subheadings.label: What Mary wanted
facts: Mary's religious aims were: to undo religious changes made since 1529, including restoring Papal authority, Catholic practices and belief in transubstantiation, and monasteries that had been dissolved; to secure a long-term future for Catholicism by marrying and having children; to ensure the Catholic religion is abided by across the country.

subheadings.label: Advisor concerns
facts: Mary's advisors were concerned about the feasibility of some of these aims. Gardiner was uncertain about restoring papal authority and the Imperial ambassador, Simon Renard, expressed concerns about trying to restore former monastic property.
Even Charles V and the pope, Julius III, were concerned that Mary would proceed too quickly and provoke unrest that might even threaten her position as queen.

subheadings.label: Parliamentary obstacles
facts: Parliament met in October 1553 but refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy, suggesting anti-Papal feeling. However it did pass the 1st Act of Repeal which restored the religious situation of 1547.
Mary used the royal prerogative to get rid of the Second Act of Uniformity and restore the Catholic Mass.

subheadings.label: The monastic land problem
facts: In April 1554 there was controversy in parliament over the issue of ex-monastic land. Landowning MPs who had benefited from the dissolution refused to reinstate the heresy laws until Mary had given them assurances regarding their land. In November Mary accepted ex-monastic land would be left. The heresy laws were then revived.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were Mary's religious aims realistic?
facts: REALISTIC: Mary used royal prerogative to restore Catholic Mass and repeal Second Act of Uniformity.
REALISTIC: Parliament passed the 1st Act of Repeal, restoring 1547 religious situation.
REALISTIC: Mary compromised pragmatically on ex-monastic land to get heresy laws revived.
REALISTIC: Many Catholics remained in the country - restoration had some popular support.
REALISTIC: Even initially-resistant Parliament eventually passed restoration legislation.
UNREALISTIC: Even Gardiner was uncertain about restoring papal authority.
UNREALISTIC: Imperial ambassador Renard worried about restoring monastic property.
UNREALISTIC: Charles V and Pope Julius III worried Mary would provoke unrest threatening her position.
UNREALISTIC: Parliament initially refused to repeal Act of Supremacy - showing anti-Papal feeling.
UNREALISTIC: Gentry vested interests in monastic land created permanent obstacles - couldn't restore monasteries.

subheadings.label: Initial welcome
facts: She was initially welcomed with great enthusiasm – bells were rung, parliament opened with a sung mass, Oxford chalices reappeared and altars and crosses were set up in London churches.

subheadings.label: Royal Injunctions of 1554
facts: The Royal Injunctions of 1554 restored some traditional Catholic practices, such as Holy Days, processions and ceremonies. It also led to the deprivation of large numbers of married clergy.

subheadings.label: Second Act of Repeal
facts: The Second Act of Repeal was passed in November 1554, which repealed all religious legislation approved since 1529. The Act protected property rights of those who had bought church land since 1536.

subheadings.label: The heresy laws and burnings
facts: Over the next 3 years, 284 Protestants were burnt at the stake under these laws; most notable Archbishop Cranmer and Bishops Hooper, Ridley and Latimer.

subheadings.label: The 12 Decrees
facts: 1556 – introduced the 12 Decrees, intended to improve clerical discipline and remove the criticisms people had against Catholicism in the first place. Decrees included bans on absenteeism, pluralism and simony.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Mary's Catholic restoration successful?
facts: SUCCESSFUL: Welcomed with 'great enthusiasm' - bells rung, masses sung, chalices reappeared.
SUCCESSFUL: Royal Injunctions of 1554 restored traditional Catholic practices, Holy Days, processions.
SUCCESSFUL: Second Act of Repeal (1554) repealed all religious legislation since 1529.
SUCCESSFUL: 12 Decrees in 1556 addressed Catholic Church weaknesses (absenteeism, pluralism, simony).
SUCCESSFUL: Large numbers of married clergy were deprived - clearing the Church of reformers.
UNSUCCESSFUL: 284 Protestants burnt at stake - including Cranmer, Hooper, Ridley, Latimer (created martyrs).
UNSUCCESSFUL: The protection of monastic land ownership compromised full Catholic restoration.
UNSUCCESSFUL: The Mass restoration depended on royal prerogative rather than full parliamentary support.
UNSUCCESSFUL: Mary's failure to produce an heir meant restoration could not be permanent.

subheadings.label: The burnings begin
facts: The heresy laws were revived in 1554 and the burnings continued from February 1555, when John Rogers was the first to be burnt, until Mary's death in 1558.
284 people were burnt at the stake (51 were women). They mostly took place in the south-east, London, Canterbury and Colchester – the Protestant strongholds.

subheadings.label: The leading Protestant martyrs
facts: In October 1555, Bishops Ridley and Latimer were burned at Oxford and in March 1556 Cranmer was burned. Before his burning, Cranmer had recanted Protestantism but on the stake he publicly reversed his recantation and denounced the Pope.

subheadings.label: Internal opposition
facts: Gardiner opposed the burnings, believing them to be counter-productive. However, his death in 1555 meant they continued apace under Pole's direction.

subheadings.label: Public reaction
facts: Large numbers attended the burnings. There isn't much evidence of the burnings converting the audience. Many people viewed them as entertainment or a commercial opportunity.

John Foxe's Book of Martyrs highlighted the burnings and coloured our understanding of the impact of the Marian persecutions. He shows there was considerable opposition to the regime. The impact on the public is not clear.

subheadings.label: The Protestant exiles
facts: During the early months of 1554 c.800 Protestants began to leave England for Germany and Switzerland. The exiles included many of the printers in England who helped develop an underground Protestant propaganda movement. They kept key Protestant works like Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were the burnings effective or counterproductive?
facts: EFFECTIVE: 284 Protestants were eliminated including key leaders (Cranmer, Hooper, Ridley, Latimer).
EFFECTIVE: Concentrated on Protestant strongholds (south-east, London, Canterbury, Colchester).
EFFECTIVE: Public attendance was large - showing state authority was visible.
EFFECTIVE: Many viewed burnings as entertainment - not converting them to opposition.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: Gardiner himself opposed them as 'counter-productive' - even regime insiders saw the danger.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: Cranmer's public reversal of recantation on the stake created powerful martyr narrative.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: 800 Protestants fled into exile - became base of Protestant propaganda.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: Exiled printers kept Protestant works in circulation - undermined the regime.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: Foxe's Book of Martyrs showed 'considerable opposition to the regime'.
COUNTERPRODUCTIVE: No evidence burnings converted audiences.

subheadings.label: Catholic worship returned quickly
facts: Edward's short reign meant that much of the country, especially the North, had always remained Catholic at a local level. Most church records identify that Catholic worship returned speedily and many welcomed it. The changes would be expensive and lengthy yet people were willing to spend their minimal funds on the Church — chalices, altars and vestments reappeared quickly in many parishes.

subheadings.label: Regional success
facts: At a local level, the Catholic restoration was more successful than the Edwardian Reformation had been. The North and West had always been more resistant to Protestant change; in these regions Mary's restoration was welcomed rather than merely accepted. Even in Protestant strongholds like London and East Anglia, many returned to Catholic practice without visible opposition.

subheadings.label: Time as the great obstacle
facts: However Mary's reign suffered the same problem as Edward's — five years was insufficient to enact lasting change. Unlike Henry and Edward, Mary faced no popular rebellion on the issue of religion itself — Wyatt's rebellion was primarily about the Spanish marriage. However over 800 clergy were deprived for failing to return to Catholic practices, suggesting a minority of committed Protestants remained.

subheadings.label: The Marian exiles
facts: Marian exiles presented a particular problem at local level.
Many were printers who had helped distribute Protestant literature, now forced into exile.
When they returned under Elizabeth, they brought radical Protestant views that clashed with moderate settlement.
These returning exiles became Puritan agitators against the Elizabethan religious compromise.

subheadings.label: Parliamentary opposition
facts: Parliament's opposition was primarily about losing land rather than the religious policies themselves — all other legislation passed without much concern. This suggests the gentry's vested interests in former church land were the main obstacle, not widespread popular opposition to Catholicism.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: By not producing an heir Catholicism did not triumph — Elizabeth would not allow it. It is worth noting that the time it took Elizabeth to establish Protestantism (she needed her own Reformation) suggests the Marian regime had been successful in restoring Catholic practice at the local level. The new clergy Elizabeth had to appoint were often reluctant converts who privately remained Catholic.

subheadings.label: Debate: What was the extent of de facto change under Mary?
facts: EXTENSIVE: Catholic worship returned speedily and many welcomed it - chalices, altars, vestments reappeared quickly.
EXTENSIVE: Catholic restoration more successful than Edwardian Reformation had been.
EXTENSIVE: North and West welcomed the restoration rather than merely accepting it.
EXTENSIVE: Even London/East Anglia returned to Catholic practice without visible opposition.
EXTENSIVE: People willing to spend minimal funds on Catholic Church items.
EXTENSIVE: Time Elizabeth needed for her own Reformation suggests Mary had been successful locally.
EXTENSIVE: New clergy Elizabeth appointed were often reluctant converts who privately remained Catholic.
LIMITED: Five years was insufficient to enact lasting change - same problem as Edward.
LIMITED: Over 800 clergy deprived for failing to return to Catholic practices - committed Protestants remained.
LIMITED: Parliament opposition primarily about losing monastic land - gentry vested interests blocked full restoration.
LIMITED: Marian exiles returned under Elizabeth and became Puritan agitators.

subheadings.label: Inflation and the Great Price Rise
facts: Inflation had been occurring throughout the 16th century, but accelerated in the 1540s. Food prices had doubled since the start of the century.

subheadings.label: Population rise (Malthusian Crisis)
facts: Population rise – Malthusian Crisis: for the first time since the Black Death the population of England was rising. From 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 million to 3 million. Agricultural productivity was unable to keep pace and therefore the price of food rose.

subheadings.label: Bad harvests
facts: Bad harvests were common. This was exacerbated by the end of the Medieval Warm Period and beginning of the Little Ice Age.

subheadings.label: Debasement
facts: Debasement: in order to finance wars against France and Scotland in the early 1540s, Henry VIII's government had begun a policy of debasement. Debasement reduced confidence in the currency and so prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the war against Scotland.

subheadings.label: Enclosure
facts: Enclosure began to pick up pace in the Tudor period due to the growing cloth market in the Netherlands. English wool was prized and so many gentry transformed their land from agriculture to livestock farming. This led to less food being produced, higher food prices, and increased unemployment.

Commonwealth men, not understanding the impact of the population rise or debasement, blamed the Great Price Rise on enclosure and greedy gentlemen. This added to the complaints that the gentry and merchant class regularly practiced rack renting and regrating to exploit the poor.

subheadings.label: Bullion from the New World
facts: Spain's conquest of the New World meant that vast quantities of American gold and silver were being imported into Europe. This meant that across Europe the value of these metals decreased and so the value of coinage decreased, exacerbating price rises.

subheadings.label: Impact: poverty and vagrancy
facts: The Great Price Rise, combined with increasing demand for land, led to high levels of poverty and vagrancy. Fears over increases in vagrancy prompted the Vagrancy Act of 1547 which condemned vagrants to two years slavery for the first offence, and lifetime slavery for a second.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did socioeconomic causes have major impact on people?
facts: MAJOR IMPACT: Food prices had doubled since the start of the century - directly affecting daily life.
MAJOR IMPACT: Population rose from 2.3 million to 3 million (1525-51) - massive demographic pressure outstripping agricultural productivity.
MAJOR IMPACT: Bad harvests common, exacerbated by Little Ice Age - food insecurity.
MAJOR IMPACT: Debasement reduced confidence in currency, prices rose to compensate.
MAJOR IMPACT: Enclosure led to less food, higher prices, increased unemployment.
MAJOR IMPACT: New World bullion devalued coinage across Europe, exacerbating price rises.
MAJOR IMPACT: High levels of poverty and vagrancy - so severe Vagrancy Act 1547 introduced slavery as punishment.
LIMITED IMPACT: Contemporaries (Commonwealth men) didn't understand real causes - blamed enclosure unjustly.
LIMITED IMPACT: Some causes were European-wide (bullion) - not unique English experience.
LIMITED IMPACT: Effects varied by region - cloth-producing areas faced different pressures from rural areas.

subheadings.label: Somerset's reputation as the 'Good Duke'
facts: Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures in 1548 – contributing to his reputation amongst the poor as the 'Good Duke'.
Somerset's proclamations and commissions to tackle enclosure raised hopes amongst the people that Somerset was their champion who would support them.

subheadings.label: Debasement continued
facts: However Somerset continued debasement to fund the war against Scotland, which increased inflation and made the economic situation worse.

subheadings.label: The harsh Vagrancy Act
facts: The Vagrancy Act of 1547 condemned vagrants to two years slavery for the first offence, and lifetime slavery for a second – a particularly harsh policy.

subheadings.label: Limited poor relief
facts: There was limited support of the poor since Henry's dissolution of the monasteries which had once provided poor relief.

subheadings.label: Weak central government
facts: The lack of a strong royal presence in the minority of Edward VI meant that central government appeared weak and more susceptible to rebellion.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were government socioeconomic policies effective?
facts: EFFECTIVE: Somerset commissioned Hales to investigate enclosures - active engagement with problems.
EFFECTIVE: Earned reputation as the 'Good Duke' amongst the poor - perceived as their champion.
EFFECTIVE: Government recognised the seriousness of the problem and took some action.
EFFECTIVE: Proclamations and commissions showed willingness to address grievances.
INEFFECTIVE: Continued debasement made inflation worse, not better.
INEFFECTIVE: Vagrancy Act of 1547 was 'particularly harsh' - slavery as punishment.
INEFFECTIVE: Limited poor relief since dissolution of monasteries - safety net gone.
INEFFECTIVE: Weak central government during minority made enforcement difficult.
INEFFECTIVE: Raising hopes amongst the poor with policies that didn't deliver led to rebellion in 1549.

subheadings.label: Scale of the unrest
facts: 1549 was a year of serious unrest across the country. Whilst the Kett and Western Rebellions were the largest, there were not the limits of the unrest. Like the Hydra of Greek mythology, cutting off one head, simply created two more. Over half the counties of England saw unrest.
1549 saw the most widespread unrest of the Tudor period. Over 25 counties saw significant unrest.

subheadings.label: The two major rebellions
facts: Kett's Rebellion in East Anglia saw 16,000 rebels gather, focused on enclosure, high rents and clerical abuses.
The Western Rebellion in Cornwall and Devon was focused on opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer enforced in early 1549.

subheadings.label: Government weakness
facts: The lack of a strong royal presence in the minority of Edward VI meant that central government appeared weak and more susceptible to rebellion.
Somerset's apparent sympathy for the commoners and the problem of enclosure had raised hopes amongst the people - feeding rather than calming the unrest.

subheadings.label: Suppression
facts: Both rebellions were ultimately suppressed by significant military force. Warwick led 14,000 troops against Kett, while Lord John Russell led 8,000 troops against the Western rebels.
However, at no point did either Kett's or the Western rebels attempt to march on London to force regime change.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: The unrest of 1549 weakened Somerset's hold of power as many in the Council blamed his policies, contributing to his fall in October 1549.

Warwick's role in the defeat of both the Western and Kett's rebellions had made him politically indispensable — he was seen as a strong leader who could restore order, paving his way to dominate the Regency Council as Duke of Northumberland.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was 1549 a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: Most widespread unrest of the Tudor period - over 25 counties affected.
SERIOUS: Over half the counties of England saw some form of unrest.
SERIOUS: Like the Hydra of Greek mythology - cutting off one head created more.
SERIOUS: Required massive military response - 14,000 troops at Kett, 8,000 at Western.
SERIOUS: Directly contributed to Somerset's fall - destabilised central government.
SERIOUS: Showed how weak central government was during the minority.
NOT SERIOUS: Neither rebellion marched on London to force regime change.
NOT SERIOUS: Different rebellions had different causes - no unified national movement.
NOT SERIOUS: Both ultimately suppressed by military force.
NOT SERIOUS: Regime survived - Edward continued, Warwick took over from Somerset.
NOT SERIOUS: Suppression in fact strengthened government - established precedent of military response.

subheadings.label: How the rebellion began
facts: The unrest began when a mob in Norfolk attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, a local gentleman. Flowerdew redirected the protest to Robert Kett, another gentleman who had also enclosed much land. Somehow Kett became the leader of this unrest. The rebels soon numbered 16,000.

subheadings.label: The rebels' demands
facts: Many of the rebels' demands were concerned with enclosure and high rents. However, there were also complaints about absent or uneducated clergy. Divisions were clear in Norwich as 6% owned 60% of the land.

subheadings.label: Events: the march on Norwich
facts: 16,000 rebels met in July 1549. They marched on Norwich – camped at Mousehold Heath. They then stormed Norwich. Kett ran a well-ordered camp – justice was administered to show they could maintain order.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: Reasons for failure: Warwick had 12,000 well-trained and experienced troops from the war with Scotland. Kett was not an experienced military leader. He abandoned his well-defended camp at Mousehold Heath to meet Warwick at Dussindale.
Government sent over 14,000 troops. Earl Warwick came and massacred the rebels at Dussindale. 3,000 were killed. A further 49 of the leaders were executed for treason.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Warwick's decisive military victory elevated him onto the Regency Council, directly leading to Somerset's fall in 1549.
The government's ability to suppress large-scale rebellion with military force shaped future responses to unrest, establishing a precedent for military suppression.
Norwich and other local authorities, influenced by Kett's Rebellion, implemented longer-term policy changes including bans on begging and organized poor relief systems.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Kett's Rebellion a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: 16,000 rebels - one of the largest Tudor rebellions.
SERIOUS: Successfully stormed Norwich, second city of England.
SERIOUS: Required 14,000 government troops to suppress.
SERIOUS: Kett ran a well-ordered camp - showed organisational capacity.
SERIOUS: Directly led to Somerset's fall - destabilised central government.
SERIOUS: 3,000 rebels killed at Dussindale - scale of suppression shows scale of threat.
SERIOUS: 49 leaders executed for treason - regime saw it as major threat.
NOT SERIOUS: Kett was not an experienced military leader.
NOT SERIOUS: He abandoned defensible position at Mousehold Heath - tactical error.
NOT SERIOUS: Massacred at Dussindale - decisively defeated once military deployed.
NOT SERIOUS: Never threatened to march on London or unseat the regime.

subheadings.label: Prelude: the murder of William Body
facts: A prelude to the unrest was the brutal murder of William Body in 1548. Body had been tasked by the government to supervise iconoclasm in Cornwall which was extremely unpopular.

subheadings.label: Religious causes
facts: There was also large opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer enforced in early 1549. Many wanted the return of the old Latin services. Partly because they did not follow the new religion and partly because many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English.

subheadings.label: Hidden socioeconomic causes
facts: The list of demands produced by the rebels are almost entirely occupied with halting religious change. However this is largely because the demands were drawn up by the local clergy who were literate. There is evidence that early demands excluded by the clergy included demands about high taxes and rents. At Bodmin the rebels would chant 'Kill all the gentlemen!'.

subheadings.label: Events
facts: The rebels initially gathered to protest the Book of Common Prayer at Sampford Courtenay. Gentry were attacked at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle. Some of the rebels marched on Exeter and besieged the city.

subheadings.label: Suppression
facts: After around a month, a government force of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay. Over 3,000 were executed.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: Failure: unlike the unrest in East Anglia, the Western Rebellion had no clear leadership. Different sections of the rebels attacked different targets. Like in East Anglia, there was limited military leadership.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Western Rebellion a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: Successfully besieged Exeter and attacked gentry across the region.
SERIOUS: William Body had been murdered by rebels - showed willingness to use violence.
SERIOUS: Took 8,000 government troops to defeat them.
SERIOUS: Over 3,000 executed - scale of suppression shows scale of threat.
SERIOUS: Rebels chanted 'Kill all the gentlemen!' - social as well as religious dimensions.
SERIOUS: Attacked gentry at multiple targets (St Michael's Mount, Bodmin, Trematon Castle).
NOT SERIOUS: Never attempted to march on London or force regime change.
NOT SERIOUS: Had no clear leadership - different sections attacked different targets.
NOT SERIOUS: Limited military leadership compared to government forces.
NOT SERIOUS: Defeated in just one month at Sampford Courtenay.

subheadings.label: The Spanish marriage
facts: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain led to concerns over a foreign marriage and that patronage would be given to the Spanish and that England would be dragged into the Habsburg's wars.
The timing of the rebellion, immediately after Mary proposed the marriage in parliament, would support this. Wyatt had previously been loyal to Mary during the Lady Jane Grey affair.

subheadings.label: Religion
facts: However xenophobia may have been a useful tool to rally mass support, hiding other causes.

Religion: the rebellion began in Kent, a more Protestant area with trading links to Protestant Northern Europe. Many of the leaders were Protestant including Thomas Wyatt. Part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth who would defend Protestantism.
The government's chronicler John Proctor blamed religion as the main cause. However he would be unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip.

subheadings.label: Political motives
facts: Many leaders of the rebellion, including Wyatt, had lost positions at court due to their faith. This was an attempt to regain their old power.

subheadings.label: Economic causes
facts: Collapse of the cloth trade in the 1550s particularly affected Kent creating some unemployment.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were religious or political motivations dominant?
facts: RELIGIOUS DOMINANT: Rebellion began in Kent - a more Protestant area with trading links to Protestant Northern Europe.
RELIGIOUS DOMINANT: Many leaders were Protestant including Thomas Wyatt himself.
RELIGIOUS DOMINANT: Plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth who would defend Protestantism.
RELIGIOUS DOMINANT: Government chronicler John Proctor blamed religion as the main cause.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Timing immediately after Mary proposed marriage in parliament supports this.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Wyatt had been loyal to Mary during Jane Grey affair - changed only after marriage announcement.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Many leaders had lost positions at court due to their faith - personal power motive.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Concerns about Spanish patronage and being dragged into Habsburg wars were political.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Proctor as government chronicler would be 'unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip' - biased toward religion explanation.
POLITICAL/MARRIAGE DOMINANT: Xenophobia may have been 'a useful tool to rally mass support, hiding other causes'.

subheadings.label: The plot
facts: A plot developed between Wyatt, Sir James Croft, and Sir Peter Carew for a four-pronged attack from Devon, Leicestershire, the Welsh borders and Kent. Having been discovered, the rebels had to act immediately. Only Wyatt in Kent did. He raised 3,000 men and began to march on London.

subheadings.label: March on London
facts: A government force led by the Duke of Norfolk was sent to face the rebels. The government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt's men declaring 'We are all Englishmen!'.

Wyatt reached the gates of London. Mary stood resolutely and refused to flee the city. She gave an impassioned speech at Guildhall which secured the support of the Londoners who refused to open the city gates to Wyatt. The royal forces, supported by the Londoners, defeated Wyatt's rebellion.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: Reasons for failure: the discovery of the plot meant the rebels were forced to rise in Winter. This meant fewer peasants were willing to join. Only one of the four forces rebelled as the other leaders got cold feet. Mary's strength and leadership ensured the rebellion was ultimately defeated.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Wyatt and the leaders were executed, and Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower.

Consequences: Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were executed. Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower, though released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture. Mary proceeded with the marriage to Philip.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Wyatt's Rebellion a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: 3,000 men raised - significant armed force.
SERIOUS: Wyatt reached the gates of London - threatened the capital directly.
SERIOUS: Government troops under Norfolk deserted and joined rebels.
SERIOUS: Rebels declared 'We are all Englishmen!' - showed broad appeal.
SERIOUS: Plot involved four-pronged attack across England.
SERIOUS: Led to executions of Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley as collateral damage.
SERIOUS: Threatened to depose Mary and replace her with Elizabeth.
NOT SERIOUS: Only one of four forces actually rebelled - others got cold feet.
NOT SERIOUS: Winter timing meant fewer peasants willing to join.
NOT SERIOUS: Mary's leadership and Londoners' loyalty defeated rebellion.
NOT SERIOUS: Mary proceeded with marriage to Philip - rebellion changed nothing.
NOT SERIOUS: Discovery of plot forced premature action - rebels unprepared.

subheadings.label: Returning Marian exiles
facts: c.800 leading Protestants had fled England at the start of Mary I's reign. In their exile they had based themselves in the Protestant hotspots of Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva where many had become more radical, educated with the teachings of John Calvin or Huldrych Zwingli.
Calvinism and Zwinglism were threats to Elizabeth as they denied the need for an episcopacy in the Church. This extended to the monarch who was said to have no role in the Church.

subheadings.label: Catholic strength at home
facts: Under Mary I's reign Catholicism had been restored to England by law. Even without this restoration, much of the English population had never left Catholicism. The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics.

Due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon, many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate and thus not the true Queen. Instead they believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England.

subheadings.label: International Catholic powers
facts: Elizabeth inherited from Mary a war with France and an alliance with Spain through Mary's marriage to Phillip. Spain and France were the two richest and most powerful countries in the world. They were both strongly Catholic.
Fortunately for Elizabeth the Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant they despised each other. Elizabeth's political future depended on this rivalry continuing.

subheadings.label: Scotland and the French complication
facts: Scotland was a complication. Mary, Queen of Scots was a Catholic monarch but had been living in France since 1548 and was married to the French Dauphin, Francis. King Henry II of France presented Mary as the true queen of England.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's own position
facts: Elizabeth was the child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. She symbolised a Protestant England and was raised Protestant. However she did not share the religious zeal of either of her half-siblings.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was foreign or domestic pressure greater?
facts: DOMESTIC: 800 leading Protestant exiles returning with radical Calvinist/Zwinglist views.
DOMESTIC: Returning exiles denied need for episcopacy and monarch's role in Church.
DOMESTIC: Catholicism legally restored under Mary - much of population had never left it.
DOMESTIC: Powerful Catholic bishops inherited from Mary held key positions.
DOMESTIC: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to Pope's stance on Henry's divorce.
DOMESTIC: Elizabeth had to choose religious settlement that would satisfy divided population.
FOREIGN: At war with Catholic France, allied with Catholic Spain through Mary's marriage.
FOREIGN: Spain and France were 'two richest and most powerful countries in the world'.
FOREIGN: French king Henry II presented Mary, Queen of Scots as true queen of England.
FOREIGN: Mary QoS married to French Dauphin - created Franco-Scottish-Catholic threat.
FOREIGN: Elizabeth's political future depended on Habsburg-Valois rivalry continuing.
FOREIGN: Pope's refusal to grant Henry's divorce gave international legitimacy to Catholic claim.

subheadings.label: Act of Supremacy
facts: The Act of Supremacy removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church.
Elizabeth was in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy consisting of Archbishops and Bishops. Mary's heresy laws were repealed – no more burnings.

subheadings.label: Act of Uniformity
facts: Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer was used in all churches. However the most radical passage the 'Black Rubric' that explicitly denied transubstantiation was omitted.
During Holy Communion, wording from both the 1552 and the more conservative 1548 Prayer Books was used. This allowed an open interpretation of Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation.
Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England church on a Sunday. Those failing to do so would be guilty of recusancy and charged 1 shilling – average weekly wage of a labourer.

subheadings.label: Royal Injunctions
facts: The Royal Injunctions: church taxes were to be paid to the Crown; the few small monasteries that Mary had managed to restore were dissolved again; the clergy were to wear distinctive vestments; music was encouraged at services and images were accepted; the clergy could marry.

subheadings.label: Via Media
facts: Elizabeth described the settlement as Via Media 'the middle way'. It was designed to be an acceptable compromise for Catholics and radical Protestants that would cease the religious conflict.

subheadings.label: Why Parliament was necessary
facts: Elizabeth could not use proclamations or decrees to enact religious change. She needed to get it through parliament to give it legitimacy and make it enforceable.
This was not anticipated to be a problem. Neither Edward or Mary had encountered significant parliamentary opposition to their religious changes.

subheadings.label: Catholic opposition in the Lords
facts: However in the 1559 parliament, the Catholic bishops and some Catholic lay nobles in the House of Lords showed they would oppose and alter the settlement. In particular making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.

subheadings.label: How Elizabeth overcame Parliament
facts: Elizabeth in response, prorogued parliament over the Easter of 1559 to delay. Elizabeth arrested two of the more vocal critics the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester for disobedience and compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor' instead.
The Settlement then passed the House of Lords by a margin of just three votes. Elizabeth was then able to remove the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

subheadings.label: Debate: Effective policy or remaining problems?
facts: EFFECTIVE POLICY: Removed Pope's authority and made Elizabeth Supreme Governor - clear Protestant break.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Strict episcopal hierarchy maintained order and royal control.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Repealed Mary's heresy laws - no more burnings, more tolerant.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: 'Black Rubric' omitted to make Prayer Book more acceptable to Catholics.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Open interpretation of Holy Communion allowed both Catholics and Protestants to participate.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Via Media designed as 'acceptable compromise' for both sides.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Settlement lasted Elizabeth's entire reign - achieved religious stability.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Elizabeth successfully managed Parliament through prorogation and arrests.
EFFECTIVE POLICY: Marian bishops removed when they refused Oath of Loyalty.
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Recusancy fine of 1 shilling = average weekly wage - financial burden on Catholics.
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Compromise satisfied neither devout Catholics nor radical Protestants fully.
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Puritans saw vestments and ceremony as Catholic remnants - ongoing dispute.
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Settlement required compromise on Elizabeth's title ('Governor' not 'Head').
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Passed Lords by margin of just three votes - extremely narrow.
REMAINING PROBLEMS: Had to arrest bishops to silence critics - heavy-handed.

subheadings.label: The historiographical debate
facts: The historian John Neale argued that a small but highly organised group of Puritan MPs — the 'Puritan Choir' — attempted to alter the Religious Settlement through Acts of Parliament. Later historians like Geoffrey Elton have questioned whether this group was as organised as Neale suggested.

subheadings.label: Strickland's Proposals (1571)
facts: Strickland's Proposals (1571): Puritan MP Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments, the ring in marriage and kneeling at communion. He was summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative and barred from Parliament.

subheadings.label: Cope's Proposals (1586)
facts: Cope's Proposals (1586): Anthony Cope MP made an extremely radical 'bill and book' proposal that would have replaced the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removed the episcopacy entirely. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London. The bill was defeated.

subheadings.label: Peter Wentworth and free speech
facts: Peter Wentworth MP was a persistent champion of parliamentary freedom of speech. In 1566 his brother Paul challenged Elizabeth's restriction of parliamentary debate. In 1576 Peter compared Elizabeth's involvement in Parliament to 'the work of the devil' — the House of Commons itself sent him to the Tower.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's control
facts: Elizabeth consistently framed religious matters as part of the Royal Prerogative — beyond parliamentary competence. Puritan MPs were never able to force lasting change through Parliament, and Elizabeth's management of the Speaker and ability to prorogue meant she retained control.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Puritan challenge in Parliament serious?
facts: SERIOUS: A small but 'highly organised group' (according to Neale) tried to alter the Settlement.
SERIOUS: Strickland tried to remove vestments and Catholic practices from Prayer Book.
SERIOUS: Cope's 1586 proposal was 'extremely radical' - would have replaced Prayer Book entirely.
SERIOUS: Wentworth's persistent challenges over free speech and religious matters.
SERIOUS: Required Royal Prerogative arguments and arrests to suppress.
SERIOUS: Repeated attempts over multiple Parliaments showed ongoing challenge.
NOT SERIOUS: Later historians (Elton) questioned whether Puritan Choir was as organised.
NOT SERIOUS: Strickland barred from Parliament, Cope sent to Tower - effectively suppressed.
NOT SERIOUS: Wentworth sent to Tower by House of Commons ITSELF - not Elizabeth.
NOT SERIOUS: Puritan MPs 'never able to force lasting change through Parliament'.
NOT SERIOUS: Elizabeth's management of Speaker and ability to prorogue meant 'she retained control'.

heading: The Puritan challenge: clergy and separatism

subheadings.label: The Vestiarian Controversy
facts: The Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised vestments (special clerical robes) worn by clergy.
Vestments signified clergy as holy men separate from lay people, which Puritans saw as Catholic error.
This seemingly minor dispute over clothing became a symbol of deeper theological disagreements.
The controversy revealed Puritan willingness to challenge Elizabeth's religious settlement.

subheadings.label: The 39 Articles
facts: The 39 Articles – these articles were the central ordinances of the new Church of England. They had been initially agreed by the Convocation in 1563 however many were resisted by Puritans as they were not seen as radical enough. In 1571 it was conceded that clergy with reservations need not follow the ceremonial articles. However all clergy had to follow doctrinal articles.

subheadings.label: Cartwright's lectures
facts: Cambridge Presbyterian professor Thomas Cartwright gave a series of lectures in 1570 strongly denouncing the hierarchy in the Church. He lost his professorship and his freedom of speech.

subheadings.label: Public appeals
facts: Admonition to Parliament – in 1572 John Field and Thomas Wilcox penned a public criticism of parliament calling for the end of Church episcopacy.
Marprelate Tracts – series of Puritan pamphlets issued 1588-89 under the pseudonym of Martin Marprelate. Alienated many moderates with their vicious and provocative attacks on bishops.

subheadings.label: Separatists
facts: Several Puritan groups attempted to establish an independent Puritan Church. 1581 Brownist Church led by Robert Browne in Norwich. 1590s a new Separatist movement was led by Henry Barrow and John Greenwood in London. The leaders were arrested and executed in 1593.

subheadings.label: Survival of Puritanism
facts: Puritanism survived through prophesyings and the classis movement as well as the protection of Privy Councillors like Leicester.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Puritan challenge in the clergy serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Vestiarian Controversy showed Puritan willingness to challenge the Settlement.
SERIOUS: 39 Articles resisted by Puritans as not radical enough.
SERIOUS: Cartwright (Cambridge professor) publicly denounced Church hierarchy in 1570.
SERIOUS: Admonition to Parliament (1572) publicly called for end of episcopacy.
SERIOUS: Separatist movements (Brownist 1581, Barrow/Greenwood 1590s) attempted to break away.
SERIOUS: Puritanism 'survived through prophesyings and the classis movement'.
SERIOUS: Protected by Privy Councillors like Leicester - had powerful supporters.
NOT SERIOUS: Cartwright lost professorship and freedom of speech.
NOT SERIOUS: Separatist leaders (Barrow, Greenwood) arrested and executed in 1593.
NOT SERIOUS: 1571 compromise on ceremonial articles defused tension.
NOT SERIOUS: Marprelate Tracts 'alienated many moderates' - undermined Puritan cause.
NOT SERIOUS: Never managed to overturn the Settlement or change doctrine.

subheadings.label: Matthew Parker (1559–75)
facts: Matthew Parker (1559–75): Parker had previously been Anne Boleyn's chaplain. He had not gone into exile during Mary's reign and was not radicalised by Calvinism or Zwinglism. He defended the Settlement by overseeing the 39 Articles at the Convocation of 1563 — resisting Puritan attempts by a single vote — and publishing his 1566 Advertisements to compromise on vestments.

subheadings.label: Edmund Grindal (1575–83)
facts: Edmund Grindal (1575–83) was unlike Parker: a former Marian exile sympathetic to Puritan concerns.
He challenged Elizabeth over her religious authority, defending prophesyings (unlicensed preaching).
His conflict with Elizabeth over religious control led to his effective sidelining as Archbishop.
Grindal's troubles showed the limits of Protestant unity within the established church.

subheadings.label: John Whitgift (1583–1604)
facts: John Whitgift (1583–1604): after her conflict with Grindal, Elizabeth needed a loyal Archbishop. Whitgift used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists and issued the Three Articles as a test — clergy had to swear that Elizabeth had sovereignty over all Church matters, that the Book of Common Prayer was the only one to be used, and that the 39 Articles were agreeable to God.

Around 300 Puritan clergy were removed by Whitgift's methods. Cecil initially criticised the Three Articles as 'too inquisitorial'. But Whitgift showed that determined repression could contain though not eliminate the Puritan challenge.

Elizabeth supported Whitgift strongly throughout his archiepiscopacy — she died holding his hand in 1603. The contrast between Grindal's defiance and Whitgift's loyalty illustrates Elizabeth's insistence on control of the Church as part of her Royal Prerogative.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were Elizabeth's archbishops effective?
facts: EFFECTIVE: Parker defended Settlement, oversaw 39 Articles, compromised on vestments.
EFFECTIVE: Parker not radicalised by exile - solid defender of Via Media.
EFFECTIVE: Parker resisted Puritan attempts at 1563 Convocation by single vote.
EFFECTIVE: Whitgift removed around 300 Puritan clergy through High Commission.
EFFECTIVE: Whitgift's Three Articles tested clergy loyalty effectively.
EFFECTIVE: Whitgift's methods 'contained' the Puritan challenge.
EFFECTIVE: Elizabeth died holding Whitgift's hand - close personal alliance.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Grindal sympathetic to Puritans, defended prophesyings.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Grindal had to be 'effectively sidelined' - failure of leadership.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Cecil himself called Whitgift's methods 'too inquisitorial'.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Could 'contain though not eliminate' the Puritan challenge - limits of power.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Grindal's troubles 'showed the limits of Protestant unity'.

subheadings.label: Limited overt challenge
facts: For the first decade of Elizabeth's reign there was limited overt Catholic challenge. This was largely due to Elizabeth's relative tolerance.

subheadings.label: Manageable punishments
facts: The heresy laws were repealed in the Religious Settlement and the sole punishment was a recusancy fine of 1 shilling. For the Catholic gentry and nobility this was a manageable punishment.

subheadings.label: Church Papists tolerated
facts: Many Church Papists attended Elizabeth's Church of England services before later attending secret Catholic services. Elizabeth and her councillors were aware of this but tolerated it.

subheadings.label: Outward conformity only
facts: Elizabeth promised that she 'would not open windows unto men's souls.' Elizabeth only demanded outward conformity. She did not persecute and even allowed northern JPs to avoid implementing recusancy fines.

subheadings.label: International factors helped
facts: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563. Philip hoped to maintain good relations with England and feared France gaining control of England should Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots come to the throne.
The Habsburg-Valois rivalry between the Spanish and French crowns prevented the great Catholic powers working together to eradicate Protestantism.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Catholic threat before 1568 serious?
facts: THREAT: Powerful Catholic bishops inherited from Mary held key positions.
THREAT: Much of English population had never left Catholicism.
THREAT: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate.
