subheadings.label: The Oxfordshire Rising (1596)
facts: The most notable example was the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — ostensibly a protest against enclosure, it came at the peak of the food crisis. The plot was discovered and the five ringleaders were publicly tried and executed as traitors. In the end only four people actually turned up — suggesting the threat of unrest was greater than the actual unrest.

subheadings.label: Government legislation
facts: Government action: the 1597 Tillage Act was passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1598 Acts for the Relief of the Poor and Punishment of Rogues strengthened poor relief. The 1601 Poor Law formalised the system, making the state permanently responsible for the poor — provisions that lasted until the mid-19th century.

subheadings.label: Local responses
facts: Local responses were often more innovative than central government — Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, had banned begging and created a community fund. The contrast between effective local action and sluggish central response revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Wheat prices doubled, oats and rye even faster.
SERIOUS: Death rate increased 50% at peak (1595-97).
SERIOUS: Food riots in multiple counties (Kent, Sussex, Somerset, Norfolk).
SERIOUS: Bands of roving unemployed men, including discharged soldiers, threatened order.
SERIOUS: Oxfordshire Rising 1596 - ringleaders executed as traitors.
SERIOUS: Inflation 'persisted into end of reign' despite earlier efforts.
SERIOUS: Required major legislation (1597 Tillage Act, 1598 Acts, 1601 Poor Law).
NOT SERIOUS: Oxfordshire Rising only had 'four people actually turn up' - threat greater than reality.
NOT SERIOUS: Government effectively suppressed unrest (executions, legislation).
NOT SERIOUS: No national rebellion emerged - localized riots only.
NOT SERIOUS: 1601 Poor Law provided lasting solution to the poverty problem.
NOT SERIOUS: Regime survived crisis - no threat to Elizabeth's rule.

subheadings.label: Managing her image
facts: As with other monarchs, Elizabeth's power relied on her image. It was important that Elizabeth seemed strong and divinely ordained. Annual Accession Day celebrations reinforced this.
In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits of Elizabeth — all had to be based on an agreed, flattering Mask of Youth template.

Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism to enhance Elizabeth's image — she holds a rainbow (symbol of peace and divine favour); on her sleeve a serpent (wisdom); her cloak covered in eyes and ears (omniscience).

subheadings.label: Challenges to her image
facts: As Elizabeth entered her 60s, her looks diminished. Her fondness for sugar had blackened her teeth; her grey hair was hidden by a bright red wig; her face was caked in white lead make-up. The cracks in the Mask of Youth were starting to show.

A series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court. Walter Raleigh's disgrace for making Bess Throckmorton pregnant damaged the courtly image. Essex's defiance and ultimate rebellion further damaged the regime in its final years.

subheadings.label: Popular criticism in the 1590s
facts: The socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s led to increased popular criticism — some commented 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'. The contrast between Elizabeth's carefully managed image and the suffering of ordinary people in the 1590s undermined her popularity.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Elizabeth's reputation managed or dangerous?
facts: MANAGED: Annual Accession Day celebrations reinforced divine ordination.
MANAGED: 1596 Privy Council order destroyed 'unseemly' portraits - controlled image.
MANAGED: Mask of Youth template ensured consistent flattering image.
MANAGED: Rainbow Portrait used sophisticated symbolism (peace, wisdom, omniscience).
MANAGED: Image of strength carefully cultivated despite ageing.
MANAGED: Smooth succession to James in 1603 - image lasted beyond death.
DANGEROUS: Looks diminished in 60s - 'cracks in Mask of Youth' showing.
DANGEROUS: Blackened teeth, grey hair hidden by wig, white lead make-up.
DANGEROUS: Raleigh scandal (Bess Throckmorton) damaged courtly image.
DANGEROUS: Essex's defiance and rebellion damaged regime in final years.
DANGEROUS: Popular criticism - 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'.
DANGEROUS: Contrast between managed image and 1590s suffering undermined popularity.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Opposing ideologies
summary: The Cold War was rooted in the fundamental incompatibility of capitalism and communism as economic and political systems.
facts: The heart of the Cold War is the clash of ideologies between Communism and Capitalism. Communism: policy that the state should own all property and industry to ensure every citizen has a fair share — based on the writings of Marx. Capitalism: policy that everyone should be free to own property and businesses, with competition in markets essential to a country's success.

The main intellectual basis of communism was constructed in the nineteenth century by Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx. Marx argued that capitalism would inevitably be overthrown by the workers in a socialist revolution, leading eventually to a true egalitarian Communist society. Lenin developed Marx's ideas for Russian conditions — founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903, which seized power in October 1917.

Under Lenin and then Stalin, the USSR became an authoritarian Communist state where the government was in charge of all aspects of the economy, there were no democratic elections and freedom of speech was limited. The state did not 'wither away' as Marx had predicted.

For the West, democracy meant the liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and a parliament elected by the people. The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a mere camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality with no extremes of wealthy capitalists and poor workers.

Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion — 'the opium of the masses'. During the revolution in Russia, churches, mosques and synagogues were closed down and religion was banned. In Europe, Christian Churches were among the leading critics of communism.

The USSR had been communist since the 1917 revolution. Capitalist America had seen the Red Scare in the 1920s and 1930s. These deep ideological differences meant that even when the two sides cooperated against Nazi Germany, fundamental tensions remained.

subheadings.label: Communism
facts: Communism was constructed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the 19th century. Marx argued capitalism would inevitably be overthrown by the workers (proletariat) in a socialist revolution, leading eventually to a classless, equal society.

Lenin developed Marx's ideas for Russia in the early 20th century, founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903, which seized power in October 1917. Under Lenin and then Stalin, the USSR became an authoritarian state with no democratic elections and limited freedom of speech.

subheadings.label: Capitalism
facts: Capitalism is an economic system based on private investment and profit. The West believed in the liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and elected government.
The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality under the dictatorship of the proletariat.

subheadings.label: Why they were incompatible
facts: Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion — Marx called it 'the opium of the masses'. During the Russian Revolution, churches, mosques and synagogues were closed down and religion was banned.

In the West, Christian Churches were among the leading enemies of communism. In 1979 the election of Pope John Paul II of Poland as head of the Roman Catholic Church strengthened political opposition to communism in Poland.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Long-term tensions 1917–1941
summary: Deep mutual suspicion between the capitalist West and communist USSR pre-dated the Cold War by over two decades.
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the subsequent Civil War (1919-22) immediately created tension with the West. Western powers including Britain, France and the USA had intervened on the side of the anti-Bolshevik Whites during the Civil War. The USSR never forgot this.

Key tensions in the 1920s and 1930s included: Soviet refusal to honour debts owed by the previous Russian government; Soviet nationalisation of the economy causing loss of foreign investment; the 1920s Red Scare in the USA; the 1919-21 Polish-Soviet War; and Soviet show trials and oppression in the 1930s.

In 1938 Western powers pursued a policy of Appeasement, signing the Munich Agreement which ceded part of Czechoslovakia to Hitler. The USSR was not consulted. Stalin interpreted this as the West allowing Hitler to expand eastwards — potentially towards the USSR.

In 1939 Stalin signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact — a non-aggression agreement with Hitler. This shocked the West and allowed Hitler to invade Poland in September 1939, starting World War Two. Stalin used the time to absorb Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.

Operation Barbarossa — the Nazi invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 — transformed the situation. The Soviets were caught by surprise and quickly in full retreat. Stalin was desperate — only the vast size of the Soviet Union prevented a German victory.

Churchill was quick to see the potential of Soviet might in Britain's war with Germany. The USSR's image was transformed in the West from a brutal dictatorship to that of patriots bravely resisting the Nazis, led by 'Uncle Joe' as Stalin came to be known. The Grand Alliance was formed out of necessity.

subheadings.label: The revolution and its impact
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917 alarmed Western powers — Britain, the USA, France and Japan had all intervened in Russia's Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites against the communist Reds.
The establishment of the Comintern in 1919 — an international organisation to promote communism — confirmed Western fears that the USSR sought to export revolution.

The 1920s and 1930s saw a 'Red Scare' in the USA as fear of communist infiltration grew. The USSR's nationalisation of the economy led to loss of foreign investment and Soviet refusal to honour debts owed by previous Russian governments.

subheadings.label: Interwar tensions
facts: Stalin's show trials and oppression in the 1930s reinforced Western perceptions of the USSR as a brutal dictatorship. The 1938 Munich Agreement (Western appeasement of Hitler) convinced Stalin that the West wanted Germany and Russia to fight each other.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 shocked the West — it seemed to confirm that communism and fascism had more in common than communism and democracy.

subheadings.label: The Nazi-Soviet Pact
facts: Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 transformed relations — Churchill was quick to see the potential of Soviet might and forged the Grand Alliance. The USSR's image was transformed in the West from a brutal dictatorship to patriots bravely resisting the Nazis, led by 'Uncle Joe' Stalin.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Wartime tensions in the Grand Alliance
summary: Despite their alliance against Hitler, the USA, USSR and Britain were divided by the second front, Poland and their competing visions for post-war Europe.
facts: Since 1941 the USSR, USA and UK had been united in a Grand Alliance against the common enemy of Nazism. However this alliance had tensions from the start: Churchill was highly anti-Communist and suspicious of Stalin's intentions in Eastern Europe; Roosevelt was also suspicious of Stalin but was equally suspicious of Churchill's imperial ambitions; Stalin was resentful to the UK and US for delaying their invasion of Nazi-occupied territory until 1944.

The Atlantic Charter (August 1941) was a joint British and American document affirming their war aims — self-determination and internal political, economic and religious freedom. It was endorsed by 126 countries including the USSR, although they were not part of writing it. This demonstrated a severe threat to Soviet ideas about how societies should be organised.

The Second Front: the USSR proposed that the Allies create a Second Front through France. They felt they had been fighting the bulk of the war in Europe alone while the Western Allies defended territories in North Africa. Churchill wanted the Second Front to be opened in the Balkans to prevent Soviet influence there. Britain and the USA stalled for several years — causing Stalin to doubt their commitment to Soviet security. The Second Front finally opened in June 1944.

Poland was deeply divisive. Poland's geographical position made it vital strategic territory for the USSR — it had been invaded via Poland three times. Britain was hosting the Polish government in exile (the London Poles) hoping to restore them to power. The West wanted a free and democratic government; the USSR saw it as a vital buffer zone. This fundamental disagreement would run from 1943 to Potsdam.

Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin in October 1944 — in which Churchill proposed dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence (e.g. 90% British influence in Greece, 90% Soviet influence in Romania) — showed that Britain was willing to accept Soviet dominance in some areas. Roosevelt was not consulted and did not approve.

When Roosevelt died in April 1945 he was replaced by Harry Truman, who was far more hostile to Stalin. unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Liberation of Europe — East vs West
summary: The different ways East and West liberated Europe from Nazi rule created fundamentally different political realities that deepened Cold War division.
facts: Allied Control Commissions (ACCs) were set up in each occupied territory after liberation, including Germany. There was a precedent that the country which had done the bulk of the liberating had more sway on the ACC. The first ACC was set up in Italy in 1943 — as the USSR had not had troops there, it was not represented.

Similarly, the Soviets dominated the ACCs in Romania, Bulgaria, Finland and Hungary — countries they had liberated. This gave them enormous practical power to shape the post-war settlement in Eastern Europe.

Partisan groups (resistance fighters fighting to liberate their own country) could also influence the post-war settlement. Yugoslavia and Albania liberated themselves via partisan forces led by Tito and Hoxha — and consequently enjoyed more freedom after the war. Poland liberated itself with the London Poles but was undermined by Soviet interference.

The USSR had liberated Eastern Europe from Nazi rule. Now Stalin sought to turn these states into a buffer zone to protect the USSR from any future invasion. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia were absorbed into the USSR. Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Albania became communist one-party states with the help of the Red Army between 1945-8.

Yugoslavia, whilst communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito. In June 1948 Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform after Tito refused to submit to Soviet direction. After 1948 the Soviet Union broke off diplomatic relations with Tito.

In 1946 Churchill declared an Iron Curtain had descended over Europe — dividing it between the capitalist West and communist East. The different experiences of liberation directly determined which side of the Iron Curtain countries would fall.

subheadings.label: Western liberation
facts: Allied Control Commissions (ACCs) were set up in each occupied territory. The precedent was that the country which had done the bulk of the 'liberating' had more sway on the ACC — so the USSR dominated ACCs in Romania, Bulgaria, Finland and Hungary.

Western liberation: in France, the Low Countries and Denmark, Allied forces were seen as liberators, bringing supplies. There was no thought of annexing territory or imposing an ideology. The situation was more complex in Greece, where Britain supported royalists in a civil war to prevent a communist state.

subheadings.label: Eastern liberation
facts: Eastern liberation: the Red Army inflicted much harsher retribution on Germany and its allies — there were terrible reprisals against civilians, widespread plunder and deportation of ethnic Germans. In annexed territories, pre-1918 Russian territories were restored to Soviet control.

Soviet political influence: the Russian forces were deeply involved in the politics of liberated countries. They supported a communist coup in Romania (1945), installed a communist-dominated coalition in Hungary, controlled Bulgaria via a Special Allied Control Council and established a National Liberation Committee in Poland dominated by communists.

By 1948, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia had been absorbed into the USSR. Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Albania had all become communist one-party states with the help of the Red Army. Yugoslavia, though communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: In 1946, Churchill declared an 'Iron Curtain' had descended across Europe — dividing the free West from the Soviet-dominated East.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The creation of the United Nations
summary: The UN was created in 1945 as an international peacekeeping organisation, but immediately became a battleground for Cold War tensions.
facts: The United Nations was established in 1945, replacing the failed League of Nations. Roosevelt had convinced the USSR to join — it was seen as a key tool for maintaining post-war peace through collective security.

The UN Security Council had five permanent members with veto power: the USA, USSR, UK, France and China. The USSR could use its veto to block any resolution it disagreed with — making the UN immediately a Cold War battleground.

The UN was immediately undermined by Cold War tensions. The USSR used its veto repeatedly to block Western proposals. The USA and its allies had a majority in the General Assembly — making the UN appear as an instrument of American foreign policy to the Soviets.

During the Korean War (1950-53) the UN authorised military action against North Korea because the USSR was temporarily boycotting the Security Council over China's representation. This was the only time the UN directly intervened militarily against Soviet-backed forces.

Despite its limitations, the UN provided a forum for dialogue and a mechanism for managing crises. It played a role in mediating disputes and providing humanitarian aid. The establishment of the UN reflected the shared hope in 1945 that a new international order could prevent another world war.

subheadings.label: What the UN was
facts: The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945, replacing the ineffective League of Nations which had failed to prevent WWII. Its headquarters were in Manhattan, New York City, reflecting the rise of the United States to global leadership.

The Security Council was the UN's most powerful body — the five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France and China) each had the power of veto. This immediately gave the USSR the ability to block any measure it disagreed with.

subheadings.label: Immediate Cold War battleground
facts: At its first meeting in 1946, the Security Council immediately became a Cold War arena. Iran raised the matter of Russian-occupied Azerbaijan; Russia countered by opening the issue of British troops in Greece. Russia used the first Security Council veto to block a plan for Britain and France to withdraw from Syria and Lebanon.

The Atomic Control Commission was created at the first UN meeting to 'deal with problems raised by the discovery of atomic energy'. The USA proposed international control of atomic weapons; the USSR rejected this as they did not yet have their own bomb and feared American dominance.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: Stalin had insisted on greater representation for individual Soviet republics in the UN, fearing it would become anti-Soviet. He eventually won representation for Ukraine and Byelorussia as separate members alongside the USSR.

Despite the Cold War tensions, the UN provided a forum for diplomacy and debate that helped prevent direct superpower conflict. It played a role in the Korean War (1950–53) when the USSR was boycotting the Security Council and the USA was able to pass a resolution authorising military action.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Iron Curtain speech and its significance
summary: Churchill's Iron Curtain speech of March 1946 gave voice to Western fears about Soviet expansionism and helped harden attitudes on both sides.
facts: In March 1946 Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton, Missouri, USA — with President Truman present. Churchill declared: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.'

Churchill warned that the Soviet Union did not want war but did want the fruits of war and the indefinite expansion of its power and doctrines. He called for an Anglo-American alliance to confront Soviet expansion.
Stalin reacted furiously, comparing Churchill to Hitler and calling the speech a call for war against the USSR. The Soviet press attacked Churchill as a warmonger.

The speech was significant because it publicly named the division of Europe and gave it the iconic phrase 'Iron Curtain'. It helped shift Western public opinion against the USSR and made the Cold War visible to ordinary people for the first time.

However its accuracy was debated — in 1946 Soviet control of Eastern Europe was still incomplete. In Czechoslovakia, for example, there had been free elections in 1946 that the Communists won with only 38% of the vote. Full Soviet control was not consolidated until 1948.

subheadings.label: What Churchill said
facts: In March 1946, Churchill made a speech in Fulton, Missouri, calling it 'The Sinews of Peace'. He coined the famous phrase: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.'

Key ideas in the speech: Europe was firmly divided; the USSR controlled all Eastern European countries equally; the West needed to negotiate from a position of strength; the USSR wanted to expand without limit and to export communism.
Churchill's key ideas: Stalin was admiring of strength and despising of weakness — the West must deal with him 'supported by the whole strength of the English-speaking world'.

subheadings.label: Reactions
facts: Reactions: Stalin reacted by accusing Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war' and arguing the USSR had only peaceful ambitions. Many in the USA thought the speech was irresponsible. Truman did not immediately signify his approval.

subheadings.label: Accuracy and significance
facts: The speech's accuracy was flawed — Soviet influence was not yet uniform across Eastern Europe. Berlin was not under total Soviet control; total Soviet domination was not yet established in Prague; Yugoslavia under Tito was resisting Moscow.

Despite its inaccuracies, the vivid image of the speech helped to encourage anti-Russian sentiment and provoked equally strong rhetoric from the USSR, ramping up tension and verbal conflict. By 1946 the mood in the USA was shifting away from isolationism to opposing communist expansion.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Soviet control of Eastern Europe — salami tactics
summary: Between 1945 and 1948, the USSR used salami tactics to install communist governments across Eastern Europe, turning it into a Soviet buffer zone.
facts: Stalin used so-called salami tactics to take control of Eastern Europe — slicing away opposition piece by piece. The method combined rigged elections, political intimidation, the merging of socialist and communist parties, and the use of the Red Army's presence as a threat.

The Baltic States — Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia — were directly absorbed into the USSR itself (not made satellite states) in 1940 during the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and again after 1945. They lost their independent governments entirely and became Soviet republics. Their populations were subject to mass deportations to Siberia.

Key Eastern European examples: Poland — January 1947, rigged elections gave Communists 80% of the vote; Romania — December 1947, King Michael forced to abdicate; Bulgaria — opposition leaders arrested and executed; Hungary — the Communist party won only 17% in 1945 free elections but by 1947 had taken full control through intimidation of the minister of the interior.

Czechoslovakia was the most significant case. In May 1946 free elections saw the Communist party win 38% — they were part of a coalition. In February 1948, with Soviet backing, the Communists staged a coup and took full control. This event shocked the West and directly prompted Congress to approve Marshall Aid.

Greece was the exception — it remained in the Western sphere. Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin in October 1944 had given Britain 90% influence there. A civil war broke out between communists and the Greek government. Stalin largely respected the Percentages Agreement and did not directly support the Greek communists — though Yugoslavia's Tito did, against Stalin's wishes.

Yugoslavia, whilst communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito. Yugoslavia had liberated itself via partisan forces and so had not been occupied by the Red Army. In 1948 Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform after Tito refused to submit to Soviet direction. After 1948, Tito-ism (the idea that national communist parties should be independent of the USSR) became a feared heresy in the Eastern bloc.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Greece and the origins of containment
summary: The Greek Civil War was the direct trigger for the Truman Doctrine — the moment America committed to containing communism worldwide.
facts: Greece had been assigned to the British sphere of influence in Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin in October 1944 (90% British influence). After liberation from the Nazis, a civil war broke out between the royalist government backed by Britain and communist partisans backed by Yugoslavia's Tito (though not directly by Stalin, who largely respected the Percentages Agreement).

By February 1947 Britain was exhausted and broke after the war. Britain announced it would need to withdraw 40,000 troops from Greece and could no longer fund the royalist government. This forced America to make a decisive choice — either step in or risk Greece falling to communism.

President Truman addressed Congress in March 1947 and announced the Truman Doctrine: the USA would contain communism wherever it threatened free peoples. He announced $400 million to support anti-communist fighters in Greece and Turkey. This was a fundamental shift from American isolationism to active global engagement.

The Truman Doctrine was deliberately broad — it committed America not just to Greece but to resisting communist expansion anywhere in the world. This was the beginning of the policy of containment that would define American foreign policy for the next forty years.

With American support, the royalist forces defeated the communist partisans in Greece by 1949. Greece remained in the Western sphere. The episode demonstrated that Britain could no longer bear the burden of resisting Soviet expansion alone — America had to take the lead.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid
summary: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan committed the USA to actively containing communism and rebuilding Western Europe economically.
facts: By 1947 President Truman was anxious about the spread of communism in Eastern Europe and believed Stalin was trying to turn the whole world communist. Western Europe had suffered huge destruction in WWII and could potentially turn to communism.

In February 1947 Britain announced it would need to withdraw 40,000 troops from Greece. A civil war was underway between communists and the Greek government. Truman decided America had to intervene — he announced the Truman Doctrine: the USA would contain communism and provide $400 million to anti-communist fighters in Greece and Turkey.

The Marshall Plan (1948): American Congress approved $13 billion of aid to Western European countries to rebuild after WWII. The top four recipients were UK, France, Italy and West Germany. The plan was explicitly designed to prevent economic desperation driving Western European countries towards communism.

Stalin was furious and criticised Marshall Aid as Dollar Imperialism, arguing that America was trying to create an empire using money. He forced Eastern European satellite states to refuse Marshall Aid — even though Czechoslovakia had initially considered accepting it.
The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid marked America's decisive shift from isolationism to containment. The USA was now committed to an active role in European affairs to prevent Soviet expansion.

subheadings.label: The Truman Doctrine
facts: On 12 March 1947, Truman appealed to Congress to strengthen non-communist forces in areas thought vulnerable to communist domination. He set out two competing ways of life: one based on free institutions, representative government and individual freedom; the other based on terror, oppression and the will of a minority imposed on a majority.

It was the policy of the USA to support free peoples who resist subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures. The USA was committed to an active foreign policy of containment — using its economic and military power to intervene in European and world affairs.

The trigger: Britain's inability to keep financing anti-communist fighters in Greece in 1947 made it clear the US needed to accept responsibility to halt communism's spread. By 1947 Stalin was not keeping to his agreements at Yalta about elections in Eastern Europe. Large communist parties existed in Italy and France.

subheadings.label: Marshall Plan
facts: The follow-up was the Marshall Plan of June 1947 — Secretary of State George Marshall offered an aid package of $13 billion to Europe. No distinction was made between 'free' and 'unfree' countries, but Stalin forbade Soviet-dominated nations to attend the Paris meeting to discuss it — 16 nations attended without them.
Stalin was furious — he labelled the plan 'Dollar Imperialism', arguing America was creating an economic empire in Europe. He feared it would pull Eastern European states out of the Soviet orbit.

subheadings.label: Soviet reaction and results
facts: Results: Most of the $12.7 billion in aid was used to purchase goods and raw materials from the USA. It supported the re-industrialisation of West Germany, promoting political stability after 1949. It strengthened anti-communist feeling in the USA and hostility in the Communist bloc.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Cominform and Comecon
summary: The USSR's response to the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan was to create two organisations to tighten its ideological and economic control over Eastern Europe.
facts: In September 1947 Stalin established Cominform (Communist Information Bureau) — an organisation that directed and controlled the leaders of the satellite states. It was Stalin's response to the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid.

Cominform required communist parties in satellite states to follow Moscow's line. It was used to purge independent-minded communist leaders — those seen as Tito-ists were expelled from communist parties across the Eastern bloc.
Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform in June 1948 for refusing to submit to Soviet direction. After this, the Soviet Union and all Iron Curtain countries broke off diplomatic relations with Tito.

In 1949 Stalin established Comecon (Council for Mutual Economic Assistance) to control the economies of the satellite states. It co-ordinated economic policy across the Eastern bloc, preventing them from trading freely with the West.

Comecon bound the Eastern European economies to the USSR, ensuring they traded on terms favourable to the Soviet Union. It was the economic equivalent of Cominform — together they ensured Soviet political and economic control of Eastern Europe.

subheadings.label: Cominform
facts: Stalin banned Soviet bloc governments from accepting Marshall Aid and called a conference of all European communist parties in Poland. From this, the Communist Information Bureau (Cominform) emerged in September 1947.

Cominform was intended as propaganda to prevent any communist party being lured by US 'dollar diplomacy'. Its aims were to 'provide information to strengthen the anti-imperialist democratic camp, the principal aim of which is to undermine imperialism, strengthen democracy and liquidate the remnants of fascism'.

The most enthusiastic party was the Yugoslav — its first headquarters was in Belgrade. However, after the rift between Tito and Stalin in 1948 and Yugoslavia's expulsion from Cominform, it moved to Bucharest. It was abolished in 1956.

subheadings.label: Comecon
facts: Tito resisted Stalin's control — he wanted to apply for Marshall Aid and refused to subordinate Yugoslavia to Moscow. When Moscow sent letters of complaint, the Yugoslavian Communist Party pointed out they had not been liberated by the Soviet Union. Tito-ists (communists who believed national parties should be independent of the USSR) were expelled from communist parties across Eastern Europe.

The Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Comecon) was formed in 1949 as an economic alliance parallel to the Marshall Plan. Initial members were the USSR, Albania, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Poland and Czechoslovakia.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Comecon helped divide Europe into two competing economic blocs. It boosted the USSR's control of its satellites — economic life was dominated by relations between Comecon members and the USSR, providing an outlet for Soviet manufacturers and a supply of raw materials. After 1956 more ambitious regional policies were attempted.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Conflicts over Germany
summary: Germany became the central battleground of the early Cold War — the two sides had fundamentally different visions for its future.
facts: Germany was divided into four occupation zones (American, British, French and Soviet) agreed at Yalta and Potsdam. Berlin, inside the Soviet zone, was also divided into four sectors. East and West could not agree on how to run a joint Allied Control Council, so they agreed to run their respective zones separately.

The two sides had fundamentally different views on Germany: the USSR wanted reparations and a weak Germany that could never again threaten the Soviet Union; the West wanted Germany to recover economically as a buffer against communism and to avoid a repeat of the Versailles cycle of humiliation and instability.

In January 1947 the Americans and British combined their zones into Bizonia. In June 1948 the West secretly introduced a new currency — the Deutschmark — into West Germany and West Berlin without consulting the USSR.

Stalin was furious at the creation of Bizonia and the Deutschmark, which he felt were attempts to intimidate and threaten the USSR. He also feared the permanent division of Germany would mean a wealthy, Western-aligned West German state on his doorstep.

Stalin chose to put pressure on the West's weakest point — West Berlin, an island of Western democracy 110 miles deep inside the Soviet zone. If the West could be forced out of Berlin, it would be a major propaganda and strategic victory for the USSR.

subheadings.label: The fundamental disagreement
facts: Germany was divided into four occupation zones agreed at Yalta and Potsdam. The two sides had very different views: the USSR wanted reparations and a weak Germany; the West wanted Germany to recover as a buffer against communism.

In January 1947 Bizonia was created from the US and British zones. In June 1948 the West introduced the Deutschmark without consulting the USSR. Stalin's key aim was to prevent the creation of a West German state.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Berlin Blockade and Airlift
summary: The Berlin Blockade (1948–49) was the first great confrontation of the Cold War — a propaganda disaster for the USSR that accelerated the formation of NATO.
facts: On 23 June 1948 Stalin imposed a blockade on all road and rail links to West Berlin and cut off its electricity. Stalin was attempting to seize control of all of Berlin. He calculated the West would not risk war to defend it.

Truman knew he could not back down — to abandon West Berlin would be a catastrophic blow to Western credibility. However he could not use armed convoys without risking war. The solution was the Berlin Airlift: Western planes supplied the city entirely by air. Stalin could not shoot them down without starting a war.

Each day 1,000 tonnes of supplies were flown in during the first month, eventually reaching 8,000 tonnes a day by February 1949. 60 B29 bombers were stationed in England as a nuclear threat. The blockade and airlift ended in May 1949 when Stalin lifted the blockade.

The blockade was a propaganda disaster for the USSR — confirming the view of Soviet aggression. It accelerated the formation of NATO in April 1949. It directly led to the creation of two separate German states: the Federal Republic of Germany (West) in May 1949 and the German Democratic Republic (East) in October 1949.

The West's willingness to risk confrontation to defend West Berlin showed the USSR that containment was serious. The Berlin crisis proved that the two sides could not work together and that Germany would be permanently divided.

subheadings.label: The Blockade
facts: On 23 June 1948 Stalin imposed a blockade on all road and rail links to West Berlin and cut off its electricity. He could not shoot down Allied supply planes without starting a war — so the Allies supplied the city entirely by air.

facts: The blockade was a propaganda disaster for the USSR — confirming the view of Soviet aggression. It accelerated the formation of NATO in April 1949 and directly led to the creation of two separate German states. The West's willingness to risk confrontation to defend West Berlin showed the USSR that containment was serious.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The creation of East and West Germany
summary: The Berlin Blockade accelerated the permanent division of Germany into two separate states with opposing political and economic systems.
facts: West Germany (the Federal Republic of Germany, FRG) was established in May 1949 from the American, British and French zones. Its first Chancellor was Konrad Adenauer. With the support of American Marshall Aid, West Germany quickly became a prosperous and democratic society.

East Germany (the German Democratic Republic, GDR) was established in October 1949 from the Soviet zone. Its first leader was Walter Ulbricht. East Germany was run as a Soviet satellite state — a one-party communist state controlled by the SED (Socialist Unity Party), formed when the USSR forced the SPD to merge with the Communists.

The contrast between the two Germanys became stark. West Germany received Marshall Aid and developed a thriving market economy. East Germany suffered from shortages of goods, lack of political freedom and Soviet-style collectivisation.

Between 1949 and 1961, one sixth of the entire East German population — around 3 million people — fled to the West through West Berlin. Many of them were skilled professionals such as doctors. This refugee crisis was also known as a brain drain. It was deeply embarrassing for communism and showed people were choosing capitalism.

The division of Germany became the most visible symbol of the Cold War division of Europe — and Berlin, with its four sectors deep inside East Germany, remained the most dangerous flashpoint for decades.

subheadings.label: West Germany
facts: When France agreed to join Bizonia (creating Trizonia) in April 1949, it was clear separate states would emerge. The West approved the Basic Law — the constitution for West Germany — in spring 1949. Elections took place in August and Konrad Adenauer became Chancellor.

West Germany (the Federal Republic) became one of the most closely controlled, economically and politically, of all the satellite states. By the 1950s it had experienced an 'economic miracle' — a developed capitalist consumer economy with trade links to the Common Market and US aid. Its leadership was unhesitatingly supportive of Washington.

subheadings.label: East Germany
facts: In East Germany, the dominant party was the SED — a coalition of former socialists and communists, in practice dominated by pro-Moscow Marxists. In May 1949 the People's Council approved a constitution. The German Democratic Republic (DDR) was officially created in October 1949.

East Germany and East Berlin remained impoverished and drab — an old-fashioned economy based on restrictive controls and wasteful production. Stalin remained uncommitted to an independent East Germany and was prepared to sacrifice it as late as 1952, when he offered reunification in return for a neutral Germany.

subheadings.label: Significance of division
facts: Fear and dislike of the SED led to the establishment of a West Berlin city government. Officially the four-power Control Commission ran the city, but West Berlin sent representatives to the Bonn parliament. East Berlin became the capital of the DDR.

West Germany and West Berlin represented the great success story of the Allies — the Nazi past was put aside, there was an economic miracle and stable, conservative politics. It became a model of capitalist development.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The East German Rising 1953
summary: The East German Rising of June 1953 was the first major challenge to Soviet control in Eastern Europe — suppressed by Soviet tanks and revealing the fragility of the DDR.
facts: The East German Rising of June 1953 was caused by strict collectivisation quotas and demands that workers increase their output by 10% without any increase in wages. Workers in East Berlin went on strike and marched on government buildings.
The protests quickly spread across East Germany. Workers demanded free elections, the release of political prisoners and the end of Soviet occupation.
Soviet tanks were sent in to crush the uprising. The East German and Soviet security forces killed at least 50 protesters and arrested 10,000 more. The rising was quickly suppressed.

The consequences were significant: the East German leader Walter Ulbricht was temporarily embarrassed but ultimately strengthened, as the USSR concluded that stability required keeping him in power; the rising demonstrated the deep unpopularity of communist rule; and the West's failure to help showed that NATO was a defensive alliance that would not intervene in the Soviet sphere.

The East German Rising was the first major popular uprising against Soviet rule in Eastern Europe — a precursor to the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 and the Czech Crisis of 1968. It demonstrated that communism had been imposed on East Germany against the will of many of its people.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: By 1953 the DDR was in serious difficulty. The Stalinist leader Walter Ulbricht had imposed harsh economic policies — collectivisation, high production quotas and low wages. The standard of living was far below that of West Germany and the 'brain drain' through Berlin was accelerating.

In June 1953, following Stalin's death in March, the Soviet leadership initially encouraged Ulbricht to adopt a 'New Course' — relaxing some of the harsher economic policies. However, Ulbricht refused to reduce the increased work quotas he had just imposed on factory workers.

subheadings.label: Events
facts: On 16–17 June 1953, workers in East Berlin went on strike and took to the streets, initially demanding the withdrawal of the increased work quotas. The protests rapidly spread across the DDR to over 400 towns and cities — around 400,000 people participated. Demands quickly became political: free elections and the end of the SED regime.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Soviet tanks were deployed on 17 June to suppress the uprising. Around 55 people were killed, 20 were executed and thousands were arrested. The uprising was crushed within days.

Significance: the East German Rising showed how shallow the roots of communism were in the DDR — workers were rising against a workers' state. The USSR's willingness to use tanks showed it would not allow regime change in its satellite states.

In the West, 17 June became a national holiday in West Germany — 'Tag der Deutschen Einheit' (Day of German Unity) — until reunification in 1990. Khrushchev subsequently supported Ulbricht's suggestion of greater controls on the Berlin border, leading eventually to the Berlin Wall.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: NATO and the Warsaw Pact
summary: The failure to agree a European peace settlement led to the creation of two rival military alliances that hardened the division of Europe into armed camps.
facts: NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) was formed in April 1949, accelerated by the Berlin Blockade. Founded by the USA, Britain, France and nine other countries. Its key principle: if any member is attacked, all will retaliate. This led to American military bases across Europe.
West Germany joined NATO in 1955 — seen as confirmation that the West was planning to create an armed and dangerous Germany again. This directly triggered the formation of the Warsaw Pact.

The Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955 as the communist equivalent of NATO — the USSR and seven satellite states (Albania, Poland, Hungary, Romania, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria). It was commanded by the Soviet Union. Seven satellite states initially signed the Treaty.

The formation of two armed blocs facing each other across Europe dramatically increased the risk that any conflict could escalate into a major war. The Warsaw Pact gave the USSR the legal justification to station troops in Eastern Europe.

NATO membership gave Western European countries the security guarantee of American military support. It tied the USA permanently into European defence — a fundamental shift from the pre-war isolationism that had contributed to the Second World War.

subheadings.label: NATO
facts: In March 1947 France and Britain signed the Treaty of Dunkirk. By 1948, fears about Soviet aggression (especially the communist coup in Czechoslovakia) led to the Brussels Pact — binding Belgium, Britain, France, Luxemburg and the Netherlands into a mutual defence pact against the USSR.

Secret talks between Britain, Canada and the USA led to the North Atlantic Treaty of 4 April 1949 — NATO. It promised consultation on issues of mutual interest and assistance in the event of an attack on any one member country. It also had an ideological element — defending not merely national security but 'freedom, common heritage and civilisation'.

NATO expansion: in September 1949 it was learnt that Stalin had atomic weapons. In 1950, communist North Korea invaded non-communist South Korea. NATO countries joined the Korean War 1950–53 to expel the North Korean invaders. In 1952 the Lisbon Conference set up a permanent HQ in Paris with a permanent military force of 35 divisions.

subheadings.label: The Warsaw Pact
facts: The Warsaw Pact was signed on 14 May 1955 by the USSR and most of its Eastern European satellites (the DDR signed in 1956). Unlike NATO, it was not an agreement between independent states — it was a policy move by the USSR in response to West Germany joining NATO.

The Warsaw Pact promised consultation on mutual interest and assistance in the event of attack on any one member. If 'a general European treaty of Collective Security' were signed — i.e. reunification of a neutral Germany — it would lapse, indicating it was more a political than a defensive move.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Though it seemed to divide Europe into armed camps, little had changed — Moscow already controlled the foreign and defence policies of its Eastern European allies. But it did mean suppression of discontent would now be by 'the Warsaw Pact' rather than the USSR alone — a convenient fiction.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Arms Race
summary: Both superpowers developed increasingly destructive nuclear arsenals, creating a world where war would mean mutually assured destruction.
facts: The Manhattan Project: the USA created atomic weapons and used them on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6th and 9th August 1945. The use of the atomic bomb ushered in the age of nuclear war and was a major threat to the USSR as they could not compete. At Potsdam, Truman used the bomb as a tool of intimidation — informing Stalin of the new weapon. Stalin felt very vulnerable and sped up his own nuclear programme.

The Baruch Plan (1946): the West called for an international organisation to monitor and regulate nuclear weapons. The Soviets rejected this as an attempt to stop them getting the bomb. Through espionage and their own independent research, the Soviet Union detonated their first atomic bomb in August 1949 — code-named First Lightning. The Americans were very surprised by the speed of Soviet development.

The Doctrine of Massive Retaliation (January 1954): Eisenhower's Secretary of State John Foster Dulles announced that America would respond to Soviet aggression anywhere with an overwhelming nuclear strike — deterring conventional attack without the expense of large standing armies. This was part of Eisenhower's 'New Look' defence policy, which prioritised nuclear weapons over costly conventional forces. The Rosenbergs — Julius and Ethel, US citizens convicted of passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union — were executed in June 1953, confirming fears of Soviet espionage at the heart of American society.

By 1955 both sides had developed a Hydrogen Bomb — 1,000 times more powerful than the original atomic bomb. In 1957 both sides developed Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles (ICBMs) capable of firing a nuclear bomb at a target 4,500km away. This led to the doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) — if either side launched a nuclear strike, the other would retaliate and both would be destroyed.

MAD made nuclear war almost unthinkable but did not end the arms race — each side feared falling behind. Each superpower constantly tried to outdo the other for fear of the missile gap. By the early 1960s 40% of the Soviet economy was spent on nuclear weapons. By the 1980s the arms race was used as a deliberate method of bankrupting the enemy — Reagan's SDI was designed to force the USSR into spending it could not afford.

The Space Race developed alongside the arms race as a more acceptable way to further missile technology and as a propaganda competition. 1957: USSR launched Sputnik, the first satellite. 1961: USSR sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit as the first man in space. 1969: USA landed Neil Armstrong on the moon — ending Soviet dominance of the Space Race.

Arms control attempts: 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty — no more atmospheric nuclear testing; 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — no more sharing of nuclear weapons; 1972 SALT I — limiting ICBMs and SLBMs; 1987 INF Treaty — destroying intermediate-range missiles. Despite these agreements the arms race continued until the collapse of the USSR.

heading: De-Stalinisation
summary: Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956 denouncing Stalin's crimes raised hopes of liberalisation across Eastern Europe — with unintended consequences.
facts: Stalin's death in March 1953 encouraged hopes for change in Eastern Europe. Communism had shallow roots in largely agrarian societies and the imposition of Soviet economic policies had caused deep resentment.

In February 1956 Khrushchev gave his secret speech at the 20th Party Congress, denouncing Stalin's crimes — the purges, show trials, cult of personality and abuse of power. This de-Stalinisation raised hopes of liberalisation across Eastern Europe.

The speech had unintended consequences — it unleashed expectations for reform that Khrushchev could not fully satisfy. What Khrushchev wanted was limited de-Stalinisation within the Soviet system, not an end to Soviet control of Eastern Europe.

subheadings.label: The secret speech
facts: Stalin's death in March 1953 encouraged hopes for change in Eastern Europe. Communism had shallow roots in largely agrarian societies, and the imposition of Soviet economic policies had caused deep resentment.

In February 1956 Khrushchev gave his 'secret speech' at the 20th Party Congress denouncing Stalin's crimes — the purges, show trials, cult of personality and abuse of power. This 'de-Stalinisation' raised hopes of liberalisation across Eastern Europe.

The speech had unintended consequences — it unleashed expectations for reform that Khrushchev could not fully satisfy. It directly contributed to the Polish October and Hungarian Uprising of 1956, as people across Eastern Europe took the speech as a signal that change was possible.

heading: The Polish Crisis 1956
summary: The Polish October of 1956 showed Khrushchev would accept limited reform to avoid full rebellion — but only up to a point.
facts: In Poland, protests began in June 1956 at the Poznan factories — initially demanding better wages but quickly becoming political. The party itself was divided; the liberal wing asserted itself.

In October 1956, party support went to Wladyslaw Gomulka — a communist who had been imprisoned from 1949 to 1954 for deviationist activities. Support for Gomulka grew in the so-called Polish October. Russian leaders criticised the Poles for anti-Soviet activity but Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than launching a massive invasion.

Gomulka proved to be a limited reformer — loyal to the USSR and to the Warsaw Pact. The Polish October showed Khrushchev would accept limited reform to maintain stability — but the limits of that tolerance would be tested immediately by Hungary.

subheadings.label: The Polish October
facts: In Poland, protests began in June 1956 at the Poznan factories — initially demanding better wages but quickly becoming political. The party itself was divided; the liberal wing asserted itself and refused to accept Russia's nominee as defence minister.

In October 1956, party support went to Wladyslaw Gomulka — a communist who had been imprisoned from 1949 to 1954 for 'deviationist' activities. Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than launching a massive invasion.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Gomulka proved to be a limited reformer — loyal to the USSR and to the Warsaw Pact. The unrest in Poland was a major factor in similar, more serious unrest in Hungary. The Polish October showed Khrushchev would accept limited reform to maintain stability — but the limits of that tolerance would be tested immediately by Hungary.

heading: The Hungarian Uprising 1956
summary: The Hungarian Uprising of October–November 1956 was the most serious challenge to Soviet control of Eastern Europe — brutally crushed and revealing the limits of Western containment.
facts: Causes: Hungary was a satellite state of the USSR and suffered as a result. Its economy was controlled by Comecon, preventing it from receiving Marshall Aid or trading freely with the West. Matyas Rakosi was a brutal communist dictator who used the AVH (secret police) to keep control — he killed 2,000 people. Khrushchev's de-Stalinisation speech of February 1956 raised hopes that life would improve. Protests for freedoms and against food shortages began.

Events: Rakosi was replaced with Imre Nagy. Nagy was a reformer and began to implement reforms — he ended the one-party state by introducing non-communists into the government, authorised the release of political prisoners and asked Khrushchev to remove Soviet troops from Hungary. Khrushchev accepted in the hope of ending the protests. However Nagy went too far by announcing Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact.

Khrushchev ordered the invasion of Hungary. 1,000 tanks rolled into Budapest. Nagy's supporters put up a fight hoping for Western aid — but none came. 3,000 Hungarians were killed. 20,000 fled to Austria. Nagy fled to the Yugoslav embassy, was replaced by hard-line Communist Janos Kadar, and was executed in 1958.

The West's failure to aid the Hungarians, despite Nagy's plea, showed that America would not interfere to defend the satellite states. America was too busy with the Suez Crisis of 1956 to intervene. This showed the West's policy of containment would not actively try to roll back communism.

The invasion secured Khrushchev's position in the USSR and the Warsaw Pact. Members knew they could not cross him. It increased tensions between the two superpowers but also confirmed the limits of Western intervention.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Hungary resented Stalinist policies and the domination of Stalinist leader Rakosi — who was heavily dependent on repression. The condemnation of Stalinism weakened the leadership. Political rallies spread and on 23 October 1956 the police fired on protesters, leading to workers joining students and intellectuals.

Imre Nagy — a previously disgraced liberal communist — took power. He began to implement reforms: ended the one-party state by introducing non-communists into government, authorised release of political prisoners and asked Khrushchev to remove Soviet troops from Hungary. Khrushchev accepted in the hope of ending the protests.

subheadings.label: Events
facts: However Nagy went too far — he announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become a neutral non-aligned country. This could cause a chain reaction across the Eastern bloc.

Khrushchev ordered the invasion of Hungary. The sheer size of the military force — over a thousand tanks deployed — made resistance impossible. Janos Kadar was appointed leader and — after seeming to be liberal — imposed Moscow's rule brutally. Nagy was executed and some 180,000 Hungarians fled to the West.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: The Hungarians had hoped for Western help but none came — the USA disapproved but did not intervene. The attention of the world was diverted by the British and French invasion of Suez in 1956. This showed that America would not interfere to defend the satellite states.

Consequences: the failure of the USA to intervene revealed the limitations of containment. There was little long-term interruption of contacts between East and West — NATO was a defensive alliance and the West had already accepted Hungary as part of the Soviet bloc.

heading: West German rearmament and NATO entry
summary: West Germany's rearmament and entry into NATO in 1955 alarmed the USSR, confirming Soviet fears and directly triggering the creation of the Warsaw Pact.
facts: The question of West German rearmament arose during the Korean War (1950–53), when it became clear that Western Europe needed stronger conventional defences against Soviet forces. The USA argued West Germany needed its own army to contribute to NATO's defence. The USSR and France were the two most strongly opposed — both had been invaded by Germany twice in thirty years.

The Spofford Compromise (1951–52): while the EDC debate continued, the USA and West Germany negotiated an interim arrangement — the Spofford Compromise — allowing limited West German troops to be contributed to NATO's European Defence Force under Allied command. This enabled rearmament to begin before the EDC question was resolved.

France initially proposed the European Defence Community (EDC) — a supranational European army in which German troops would serve under an integrated European command rather than as a separate national army. France then rejected it in August 1954, fearing German dominance. West Germany was subsequently invited to join NATO directly.

Stalin's Peace Note (March 1952): in a diplomatic move timed to derail Western plans, Stalin proposed a unified, democratic and neutral Germany — free elections, withdrawal of all occupation forces, and no alliance obligations. The West rejected the offer, fearing a neutral Germany would eventually drift towards the USSR and that reunification would threaten West German integration into NATO. Adenauer himself opposed reunification if it meant leaving the Western alliance. Historians debate whether Stalin's offer was genuine or a propaganda manoeuvre.

West Germany joined NATO in May 1955 with a new army — the Bundeswehr — limited in size, prohibited from developing nuclear weapons, and permanently under NATO command. The Soviet reaction was immediate — the Warsaw Pact was formed one week later.

The Hallstein Doctrine (1955): the West German government declared that recognising the GDR constituted an unfriendly act towards the Federal Republic — West Germany would break off diplomatic relations with any country that recognised East Germany. The only exception was the USSR itself (the 'Moscow exception'). The Doctrine formalised West Germany's refusal to accept the legitimacy of the communist East German state and remained policy until Brandt's Ostpolitik dismantled it in 1969.

subheadings.label: The pressure for rearmament
facts: The Korean War (1950–53) demonstrated that the West needed more conventional ground forces in Europe — Western Europe could not be defended against the Red Army without a contribution from West Germany. The Spofford Compromise (1951–52) allowed limited German troops under Allied command as an interim measure while the wider debate continued.
France proposed the European Defence Community as an alternative to a sovereign German army. When France rejected its own plan in 1954, the path was cleared for direct West German NATO membership.

subheadings.label: Stalin's Peace Note
facts: In March 1952 Stalin offered a unified, democratic and neutral Germany — free elections, all occupation forces withdrawn, no alliance obligations. The West rejected the offer, fearing a reunified but neutral Germany would eventually fall into the Soviet orbit and that the offer was a propaganda manoeuvre to derail West German NATO integration. Adenauer, whose political strategy depended on West Germany's Western alignment, was particularly opposed.

Historians remain divided: some (like Wilfried Loth) argue it was a genuine offer; others (like Rolf Steininger) argue Stalin never intended to deliver free elections. The rejection remains one of the great 'what-ifs' of the Cold War.

subheadings.label: The Hallstein Doctrine and its significance
facts: The Hallstein Doctrine (1955) made West Germany's non-recognition of the GDR an explicit foreign policy — any state recognising East Germany would lose its diplomatic relations with the FRG. It reflected West Germany's position that only the Federal Republic could speak for all Germans. It was abandoned by Brandt's Ostpolitik after 1969, when the Basic Treaty recognised the GDR as a separate sovereign state.

West German NATO entry dramatically increased Cold War tensions. From the Soviet perspective, the Western powers had created a rearmed Germany within NATO — exactly the scenario they had fought to prevent.

heading: The Berlin Wall
summary: The Berlin Wall of August 1961 halted the brain drain from East Germany — a propaganda disaster that confirmed communism's failure.
facts: Causes: with the support of American Marshall Aid, West Germany was becoming prosperous and democratic. Meanwhile East Germany suffered from shortages and lack of political freedom. Between 1949 and 1961 one sixth of the entire East German population — around 3 million people — fled to the West through West Berlin. Many were skilled professionals — a brain drain that was embarrassing for communism.

Khrushchev issued the Berlin Ultimatum in 1958 — giving the West 6 months to leave West Berlin and allow it to become a free city. Several summit meetings failed to resolve the issue: the Paris Summit of 1960 collapsed over the U2 spy plane incident; the Vienna Summit of 1961 with Kennedy failed when Khrushchev tried to bully the new young president.

Walter Ulbricht, the communist leader of East Germany, pleaded with Khrushchev to act. On 13th August 1961 a barbed wire fence was constructed overnight around West Berlin. It was later fortified with concrete and traps to prevent people escaping — becoming the Berlin Wall. German families and friends were separated overnight, not to be reunited for 28 years. Those attempting to cross were shot, like 18-year-old Peter Fechter.
In October 1961 a standoff occurred between US and Soviet tanks on either side of Checkpoint Charlie for hours — the closest the Berlin crisis came to direct military confrontation.

The Wall was a short-term success for Khrushchev — the refugee crisis was halted and the East's economy could recover. But it became a propaganda disaster: Kennedy visited Berlin in 1963 and made his Ich bin ein Berliner speech, and the Wall became a worldwide symbol of Soviet oppression.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Khrushchev needed to show the world — and the critical Chinese communists — that Soviet economic policies worked. Yet in East Germany they were obviously failing. The 'brain drain' could not continue.

In 1958 Khrushchev issued his Berlin Ultimatum — the Western Allies had 6 months to leave Berlin and declare it a 'free city', or he would hand control of transport links to the East German government. Summit meetings 1959–61 failed to resolve the issue. The Paris summit (1960) collapsed when a US U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR.

Ulbricht and his colleagues may have taken the decision on 12 August 1961. The frontier was closed that night and barriers erected, leading to the building of a wall on 17 August. A second, inner wall was constructed in 1962 with a 'zone of death' between. Some 5,000 managed to escape up to 1989 and there were possibly 136 deaths among those attempting to escape.

subheadings.label: Construction
facts: Significance: the Wall was, in the view of US Secretary of State Dean Rusk, 'a monument to communist failure'. It was not to separate East from West but to keep East Germans from defecting. Kennedy increased troop numbers and made his famous speech in Berlin in June 1963: 'Ich bin ein Berliner'.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: The Wall confirmed the existing status quo in Europe and ended any hopes that détente might lead to fundamental change. It showed that communist leaders were now wedded to defence of a failing system rather than resolving problems by expansion.

heading: The Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other point — resolved through secret diplomacy and mutual compromise.
facts: Causes: Cuba had been a pro-American dictatorship under Batista. In 1959 Fidel Castro overthrew Batista in the Cuban Revolution and nationalised American land and companies. America boycotted Cuban sugar — Castro was driven into the arms of Khrushchev. In April 1961 the CIA-trained Bay of Pigs invasion by 1,400 Cuban exiles was a total failure, humiliating America. Castro realised he was vulnerable and sought further Soviet help. Khrushchev wanted America to feel threatened — just as US missiles in Turkey threatened the USSR.

Crisis: Soviet missiles in Cuba were spotted by a U2 spyplane on 14th October 1962. Kennedy convened ExComm to review his options: military attack would result in world war and MAD; diplomacy was seen as weak. Kennedy opted for a naval blockade — the missiles were not yet operational. What followed was 13 days of crisis with ships getting closer and closer to the blockade.

On 24th October the Soviet ships reached the blockade and stopped. They eventually turned around — Khrushchev blinked. On 27th October a U2 spyplane was shot down over Cuba — Kennedy's advisors suggested he attack but Kennedy refused. On 28th October the crisis ended: America agreed to secretly remove missiles in Turkey and not invade Cuba if Soviet missiles were publicly removed from Cuba.

Consequences for Khrushchev: America had been forced to remove its Jupiter missiles in Turkey; Cuba remained communist. Consequences for Kennedy: he was seen to have won — Khrushchev backed down first; could save face by removing Turkish missiles secretly; was seen as strong. Khrushchev was humiliated and ousted in 1964, replaced by Brezhnev.

Attempts to avoid nuclear confrontation followed: 1963 nuclear hotline established between Washington and Moscow; 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty — no more atmospheric nuclear testing; 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — no more sharing of nuclear weapons with other countries.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Cuba had been a US ally until Fidel Castro's communist revolution in 1959. The USA sponsored the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961 — an attempt to overthrow Castro by CIA-trained Cuban exiles. Khrushchev placed nuclear missiles in Cuba to defend it and to counter US Jupiter missiles in Turkey which were a direct threat to the USSR.

In October 1962 a U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile installations in Cuba. Kennedy was presented with two options: an air strike to destroy the missiles, or a naval blockade ('quarantine'). Kennedy chose the blockade and demanded the missiles be removed.

subheadings.label: The crisis
facts: For 13 days the world held its breath as Soviet ships carrying missiles approached the US quarantine line. Soviet submarines were in the area. Kennedy and Khrushchev exchanged letters — Khrushchev eventually offered to remove the missiles if the USA pledged not to invade Cuba.

A second letter from Khrushchev added a demand that US Jupiter missiles be removed from Turkey. Kennedy publicly accepted the pledge not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove the Turkish missiles.

subheadings.label: Resolution
facts: Consequences for Khrushchev: America had been forced to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey; Cuba remained communist and America would not invade. However Khrushchev was seen to have backed down first and was ousted in 1964, replaced by Brezhnev.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Consequences for Kennedy: seen to have 'won' — Khrushchev backed down and the Cuban missiles were removed. Kennedy was seen as strong and having stood up to Khrushchev. Consequences for both: 1963 — nuclear 'hotline' established. 1963 — Limited Test Ban Treaty. 1968 — Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The crisis made both sides more determined to avoid future nuclear confrontations.

heading: The Space Race
summary: The Space Race became a key arena of Cold War competition — a battle for technological prestige that the USSR initially led but the USA ultimately won.
facts: The Space Race grew out of the arms race — missile technology underpinned both. The early 1950s saw considerable US interest in space and science fiction, which reflected fears of communism and the infiltration of an 'alien' ideology into US life.

Sputnik, October 1957: despite a lot of US research, it was the USSR that made the first major advance into space — launching the first man-made satellite. Sputnik circled the Earth once every 90 minutes at a speed of 28,000 miles an hour. This shocked the USA — it showed Soviet technology was no longer lagging behind and that a Russian satellite crossing the USA could theoretically be weaponised.

The USSR continued to lead: in November 1957 they put a dog (Laika) into space. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1. The first woman in space was Valentina Tereshkova (June 1963) and the first spacewalk was by Alexei Leonov (March 1965).

US response: the USA formed NASA using the rocket knowledge of German scientist Werner von Braun. In February 1962 John Glenn made a successful voyage in space. Kennedy made the challenge explicit in September 1962, pledging to put a man on the moon by the end of the decade.

US achievement: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the moon on 20 July 1969. The considerable resources taken by this Race and the efforts to control the parallel arms race by the SALT led to greater cooperation.

The first joint US–Soviet space mission — the Apollo-Soyuz Mission — took place in 1975, symbolising the spirit of détente. The Space Race led to considerable excitement about the possibilities of space travel, heroism and technological advances.
